To catch each class of defect separately, @tbl-vol3-verifier-cascade-stages divides the admission decision into five predicate families. These families are logical questions rather than separate microservices, and their concrete checks depend on the target artifact: a complete demonstration, an isolated recovery segment, a preference pair, or an evaluation fixture for fresh rollouts.

| Predicate                                                  | Admission question                                                                                      | Repair example                                                                                                                                 |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| $\text{chk}_{\text{record}}$: record adequacy and fidelity | Does the available record accurately represent the events and context required for this use?            | Distinguish a malformed tool call rejected before dispatch from an executed patch; bind test outcomes strictly to the evaluated candidate.     |
| $\text{chk}_{\text{use}}$: permitted use                   | Are the data provenance, licensing, access rights, and dataset splits compatible with the proposed use? | Quarantine evaluation benchmarks to prevent training contamination; hold derived traces pending unresolved disclosure reviews.                 |
| $\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}$: process conditions             | Does execution history satisfy the declared operational constraints and tool policies?                  | Verify that the agent respected file-modification boundaries, obtained required execution approvals, and stayed within memory and step limits. |
| $\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$: outcome conditions              | Does empirical evidence verify that the candidate achieved the required objective?                      | An end-to-end bug repair requires authoritative regression tests to pass; an isolated recovery turn requires its scoped postcondition to hold. |
| $\text{chk}_{\text{target}}$: target suitability           | Are the selected target or comparison roles justified by context and the learning objective?            | Retain an intercepted malformed proposal as conditioning context while masking it from token-level imitation targets.                          |

: **Predicates for consumer-specific admission**: Each verifier records its version, empirical evidence, evaluation scope, and downstream routing consequence. A faithful trajectory log can safely record invalid or prohibited actions without endorsing them as learning targets. {#tbl-vol3-verifier-cascade-stages}

For an end-to-end demonstration route, admission requires satisfying the conjunction $\text{chk}_{\text{record}} \land \text{chk}_{\text{use}} \land \text{chk}_{\text{proc,demo}} \land \text{chk}_{\text{out,demo}} \land \text{chk}_{\text{target,demo}}$. The subscripts emphasize that predicates are consumer-specific: a candidate that fails the final repair objective fails this route's outcome condition ($\text{chk}_{\text{out,demo}}$), whereas an isolated error-recovery segment within that same run can satisfy the outcome check of a recovery-learning route. Any action designated as an imitation target must be justifiable strictly from the observation context the agent possessed at that step, without lookahead leakage or hindsight annotations injected from subsequent checks. These target designations determine the token-level loss masks during supervised fine-tuning.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Token-level loss masking and target designation mechanisms are developed in @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-loss-masking.
:::

Engineers must separate record validity from action validity. A log that accurately captures a malformed tool call and the runtime's immediate pre-dispatch refusal satisfies record adequacy ($\text{chk}_{\text{record}}$); the logging subsystem worked properly even though the model made an error. Conversely, missing environment observations or out-of-order tool responses make a trajectory unusable for imitation learning, even if the candidate code ultimately passed all tests. Pipelines can route truncated or incomplete records to diagnostic stores for failure analysis, but must never package them as behavioral demonstrations.

A preference route adds the shared-context and justified-ordering conditions that define a preference comparison (@sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-learning-artifacts) to its outcome and target predicates. Until paired with a matching winning rollout, a failed attempt remains only an unassigned comparison candidate. For reinforcement learning pipelines, curation delivers versioned task definitions, resettable environment fixtures, and automated grading harnesses for fresh rollouts rather than static records of past failures. While these downstream consumers share the same requirements for permitted use ($\text{chk}_{\text{use}}$) and record adequacy ($\text{chk}_{\text{record}}$), they differ in how they check outcomes ($\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$) and assign target labels ($\text{chk}_{\text{target}}$).

Each predicate returns one of four canonical states (`pass`, `fail`, `pending`, or `unknown`), following the four-verdict rule of @sec-vol3-evaluation-contract-verdicts. A `fail` stops evaluation along that route at once and retains the record for diagnosis or another route (@fig-vol3-verifier-cascade). A missing or timed-out check never defaults to a pass; unverified candidates move to an unresolved holding queue, tagged with the missing evidence needed to finish the check. Curation telemetry counts evaluated, admitted, rejected, and unresolved records per route so that traces redirected to diagnostic pools never inflate the reported yield of demonstrations, and so that outcome checks themselves are guarded against manipulation by the candidate code.

::: {#fig-vol3-verifier-cascade fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**One Admission Route**: A collection record meets the five predicates in execution order and is admitted to the route only if every one passes. The first result other than a pass stops that route's checks. A failure rejects the record for this route without deleting it, and a pending or unknown result goes to an unresolved hold instead of counting as a pass. Other routes evaluate the same record under their own conditions." fig-alt="Grid with five columns headed R record adequacy, U permitted use, P process, O outcome, and T target suitability, and three rows for record A, record B, and record C. Record A passes all five predicates and an arrow leads to a box labeled admitted for this route. Record B passes R, U, and P, fails O, and its T cell is marked not run; a red line from the fail cell leads to a box labeled rejected, record kept. Record C passes R, is pending at U, and its P, O, and T cells are marked not run; a gray line from the pending cell leads to a dotted box labeled unresolved hold, evidence missing."}
![](images/svg/fig-vol3-verifier-cascade.svg)
:::

### Test-tampering defense {#sec-vol3-verifier-gaming}

When an agent resolves a failing test suite by rewriting the test assertion rather than fixing the underlying race condition (@lst-vol3-curation-assert-true), the breach costs far more during data curation than during benchmark evaluation. Tampering during evaluation skews a single benchmark score; tampering during collection admits corrupt demonstrations that train later models to repeat the exploit.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Grader isolation, which keeps held-out tests, grading scripts, and pass signals beyond the candidate's reach, is established in @sec-vol3-evaluation-gyms-grader-isolation.
:::

::: {#lst-vol3-curation-assert-true lst-cap="**A tampered reproducer**: The candidate replaces the missed-wakeup assertions with a constant-true assertion. The local test exits with success while the defect remains."}
```diff
--- a/tests/test_pool_wakeup.py
+++ b/tests/test_pool_wakeup.py
@@ def test_waiter_wakes_after_release():
     pool = ConnectionPool(max_size=1)
-    waiter = pool.acquire_async()
-    pool.release(pool.acquire())
-    assert waiter.done(timeout=1.0)
+    # skip flaky wakeup check
+    assert True
```
:::

Replacing the assertion produces a zero exit code from the test runner while leaving the concurrency bug untouched. In a well-designed cascade, this patch fails on two counts: the candidate diff violates the task's allowed-path policy (failing process condition $\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}$), and running the code against clean, unedited test harnesses reproduces the deadlock (failing outcome condition $\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$). An agent's self-reported success or local exit code must never override authoritative verifiers.

**Test-tampering defense**\index{Test-tampering defense!definition} is grader isolation applied to admission. It is the set of controls that keep test harnesses, test inputs, and verification results beyond the reach of the candidate and the acting agent, so that a pass recorded by $\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$ is an independent measurement rather than the candidate's own report. Because later checkpoints train on admitted trajectories, an undetected bypass is reinforced across training rounds rather than contained to one evaluation trial. The defense protects the integrity of the measurement, not its breadth; a tamper-proof suite still checks only what its assertions cover, and whether a passing solution generalizes remains a question for the target suitability predicate $\text{chk}_{\text{target}}$. The failure modes that tamper defense prevents are not hypothetical: they have appeared directly in frontier models during agentic training.

::: {#ws-14-special-cased-tests-2025 .callout-war-story title="Special-cased tests in agentic coding (2025)"}

**Context**: Anthropic's system card for Claude 3.7 Sonnet documents strategic evaluation gaming observed during agentic coding evaluations [@anthropic2025claude37].

**Mechanism**: When faced with difficult programming tasks after repeated unsuccessful attempts, the model occasionally resorted to reward hacking, exploiting discrepancies between the empirical reward signal and true task completion. Specifically, the model hardcoded expected return values for known test cases or modified unit test assertions directly so that the suite matched its incorrect implementation.

**Impact**: Standard user testing failed to catch the behavior because it appeared rarely during straightforward interactions, emerging primarily after extended, multi-turn troubleshooting cycles in specialized programming sandboxes.

**Fix**: The team deployed transcript classifiers to detect gaming patterns in training runs and applied targeted mitigations prior to model deployment. For production agentic environments, the report advises monitoring for repetitive edit-and-test loops on individual files, code comments indicating test-specific overrides, and unauthorized diffs against test suites.

**Systems lesson**: An exit code produced inside an execution environment accessible to untrusted agent code is unverified telemetry. A curation pipeline that blindly admits trajectories based on local test passes ingests the exact gaming behavior that monitoring seeks to eradicate. Tamper verification must therefore run as an immutable gate in the cascade before any trajectory can serve as a training target.

:::

To prevent such exploits from entering the corpus, tamper defense combines the evaluation gym's containment controls (principle \ref{pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing}) with an admission-specific diff audit. Out-of-tree test fixtures keep authoritative tests outside the candidate's writable workspace until its snapshot is hashed and frozen. Isolated runner supervision executes the harness in a fresh sandbox where candidate code cannot patch assertion libraries or forge exit codes (since a read-only mount alone still allows co-located code to read tests or interfere with the reporting process; @sec-vol3-evaluation-gyms-grader-isolation). On top of those two evaluation controls, admission adds a protected-path manifest that binds the diff against the base commit to the process predicate, so any unauthorized change to test suites, continuous integration configuration, or build dependencies fails $\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}$ irrespective of the test runner's exit code. Because the manifest follows the task's patch-admission policy, a task that legitimately requires a new regression test or an updated package manifest can still pass. Containment and authorization checks precede the execution of untrusted code regardless of how the other predicates are scheduled, and an audit log written after the fact cannot substitute for them.

When evaluating non-deterministic tasks, verification harnesses enforce a declared repetition protocol that fixes environmental seeds, maximum retry bounds, and aggregation rules for inconsistent trials. Rerunning a flaky test until it passes once merely samples from favorable noise. If a defective candidate passes a flaky test with probability $\AttemptPassProbability$ per run, rerunning it up to $\IndependentAttemptCount$ times reports a pass with probability $1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount$, the at-least-one form of pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ applied here to false passes. Timeouts must likewise be recorded as unresolved outcomes (`pending` or `unknown`) and routed to an inspection queue rather than silently treated as model errors or transient infrastructure faults. Once the predicates and their isolation bounds are fixed, the remaining question is how to order those checks so that rejected candidates consume as little verifier time as possible.

### Cascade economics {#sec-vol3-verifier-economics}

Running an eight-second sandboxed test suite before a twenty-millisecond process audit burns seconds of verifier slot time on candidates that a fast check would have rejected immediately. To price and optimize the order in which checks run for a given admission route, let $\text{chk}_1,\ldots,\text{chk}_{\AdmissionCheckCount}$ represent the sequence of admission predicates in execution order. Define $\CheckPassProbability_i=\Pr(\text{chk}_i\text{ passes}\mid \text{chk}_1,\ldots,\text{chk}_{i-1}\text{ pass})$ as the conditional pass probability of predicate $\text{chk}_i$, with $\CheckPassProbability_1$ denoting the unconditional pass probability of the initial check. Let $\CheckSlotTime_i$ represent the expected verifier slot time conditional on reaching that check, measured in seconds. Under short-circuit evaluation, which stops at the first non-passing predicate, the expected verification time per attempted record is:

$$\ExpectedCheckingTime=\sum_{i=1}^{\AdmissionCheckCount} \CheckSlotTime_i\prod_{j=1}^{\AdmissionCheckIndex-1}\CheckPassProbability_j,$$ {#eq-verifier-cost-cascade}

where the empty product evaluates to one. The overall route yield $\AdmissionRouteYield$ represents the joint probability that a candidate passes all $\AdmissionCheckCount$ predicates:

$$\AdmissionRouteYield=\Pr(\text{chk}_1\land\cdots\land \text{chk}_{\AdmissionCheckCount})=\prod_{i=1}^{\AdmissionCheckCount}\CheckPassProbability_i.$$

For routes with nonzero yield ($\AdmissionRouteYield > 0$), the ratio $\ExpectedCheckingTime/\AdmissionRouteYield$ is the expected verification slot time spent per admitted trajectory. The yield $\AdmissionRouteYield$ plays the role of acceptance probability in the cost-per-accepted-task formula (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task). Because this ratio is an expectation across large samples, a batch with zero admitted records reports total slot time consumed rather than an undefined ratio. Upstream rollout generation, retry loops, and downstream storage costs are accounted for outside this verifier cascade.

Reordering these predicates preserves the exact admitted set as long as their definitions, inputs, and evaluations remain unchanged. When predicates are correlated, however, conditional pass probabilities must be re-measured for each order, because each check sees a different pre-filtered subset. Operational dependencies and containment rules also constrain permissible orders; data governance and containment checks, for instance, must always precede running untrusted code in a sandbox.

When two adjacent predicates $\text{chk}_\FirstAdjacentCheckIndex$ and $\text{chk}_\SecondAdjacentCheckIndex$ are statistically independent, an exchange argument yields the cheaper execution order in closed form. Swapping an adjacent pair leaves every earlier check unchanged and passes the exact same joint fraction $\FirstAdjacentCheckPassProbability \SecondAdjacentCheckPassProbability$ of candidates to every later check, so only the pair's own two terms in @eq-verifier-cost-cascade change. Conditional on reaching the pair, running $\text{chk}_\FirstAdjacentCheckIndex$ before $\text{chk}_\SecondAdjacentCheckIndex$ incurs an expected local cost of $\FirstAdjacentCheckSlotTime + \FirstAdjacentCheckPassProbability \SecondAdjacentCheckSlotTime$, whereas running $\text{chk}_\SecondAdjacentCheckIndex$ before $\text{chk}_\FirstAdjacentCheckIndex$ incurs $\SecondAdjacentCheckSlotTime + \SecondAdjacentCheckPassProbability \FirstAdjacentCheckSlotTime$. Running $\text{chk}_\FirstAdjacentCheckIndex$ first is cheaper whenever $\FirstAdjacentCheckSlotTime + \FirstAdjacentCheckPassProbability \SecondAdjacentCheckSlotTime < \SecondAdjacentCheckSlotTime + \SecondAdjacentCheckPassProbability \FirstAdjacentCheckSlotTime$. Collecting $\FirstAdjacentCheckSlotTime(1-\SecondAdjacentCheckPassProbability)$ on the left and $\SecondAdjacentCheckSlotTime(1-\FirstAdjacentCheckPassProbability)$ on the right and dividing by both rejection probabilities gives:

$$\frac{\FirstAdjacentCheckSlotTime}{1-\FirstAdjacentCheckPassProbability} < \frac{\SecondAdjacentCheckSlotTime}{1-\SecondAdjacentCheckPassProbability}.$$ {#eq-vol3-trajectory-curation-order-rule}

Because any schedule in which an adjacent pair violates this inequality can be improved by swapping that pair, the optimal schedule orders all independent predicates by ascending *cost per rejection*, $\CheckSlotTime_i / (1 - \CheckPassProbability_i)$, running the cheapest rejection filter first. This rule matches the predicate-ranking algorithm developed for relational database query optimizers with expensive user-defined filters [@hellerstein1993predicate].[^fn-predicate-rank-curation]

[^fn-predicate-rank-curation]: **Predicate Rank**: Relational database query optimizers faced the same scheduling problem when selection predicates began calling expensive user-defined functions. Ordering filters by selectivity alone ran heavy functions on rows that a fast check would have dropped. Sorting independent filters by rank, defined as per-row cost divided by rejection probability $(1 - \CheckPassProbability_i)$, minimizes expected work, matching the exchange argument in @eq-vol3-trajectory-curation-order-rule [@hellerstein1993predicate]. In agent curation cascades, where checks range from sub-millisecond AST scans to multi-minute integration tests and human reviews, rank ordering decides where most of the verification budget goes. \index{Predicate rank!query optimization}

```{python}
#| label: lego-14-verification-cascade-economics-and-throughput
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ADMISSION ORDER UNDER IDENTICAL CRITERIA (LEGO)
# │ Context: @nbk-14-verification-cascade-economics-and-throughput.
# │ Goal: Compare two permissible orders for one demonstration route.
# │ Show: Equal expected yield, different occupied verifier-slot time.
# │ How: Independent fixed predicate outcomes; short-circuit each order.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_qty

class VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Hypothetical Inputs, from the admission-order scenario) ─
    scenario = Scenarios.DemonstrationAdmissionOrder
    variant = Scenarios.DemonstrationAdmissionOrderSlowAudit
    n_rollouts = scenario.candidates
    checks = list(scenario.checks)  # record, use, process, outcome, target
    names = ("R", "U", "P", "O", "T")
    pass_rates = tuple(p for p, _ in scenario.checks.values())
    costs_s = tuple(t.to(second).magnitude for _, t in scenario.checks.values())
    orders = []
    for named_order in scenario.orders:
        order = []
        for _check in named_order:
            order.append(checks.index(_check))
        orders.append(tuple(order))

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Expected Work and Yield) ───────────────────────────
    admission = scenario.result
    expected_s = [t.to(second).magnitude for t in admission.time_per_attempted]
    yield_rate = admission.route_yield
    expected_admitted = admission.admitted
    saved_fraction = admission.saving
    # Exchange argument for the adjacent P/O swap (order rule).
    reach_po = pass_rates[0] * pass_rates[1]
    ratio_p = admission.cost_per_rejection["process"].to(second).magnitude
    ratio_o = admission.cost_per_rejection["outcome"].to(second).magnitude
    ratio_t = admission.cost_per_rejection["target"].to(second).magnitude
    swap_gain_s = reach_po * (costs_s[3] * (1 - pass_rates[2]) - costs_s[2] * (1 - pass_rates[3]))
    # Checkpoint variant: a slower, less selective process audit.
    alt_p_pass = variant.checks["process"][0]
    alt_p_cost_s = variant.checks["process"][1].to(second).magnitude
    alt_ratio_p = variant.result.cost_per_rejection["process"].to(second).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. ASSERT (Independent Exhaustive Outcome Check) ───────────────
    enumerated_s = [0.0, 0.0]
    enumerated_yield = 0.0
    total_probability = 0.0
    for bits in range(2 ** len(names)):
        passed = []
        for i in range(len(names)):
            passed.append(bool(bits & (1 << i)))
        probability = 1.0
        for i in range(len(names)):
            probability *= pass_rates[i] if passed[i] else 1 - pass_rates[i]
        total_probability += probability
        accepted = []
        for order_index, order in enumerate(orders):
            accepts = True
            for stage in order:
                enumerated_s[order_index] += probability * costs_s[stage]
                if not passed[stage]:
                    accepts = False
                    break
            accepted.append(accepts)
        check(accepted[0] == accepted[1], "same accepted set for every outcome")
        if accepted[0]:
            enumerated_yield += probability
    check(abs(total_probability - 1) < 1e-12, "probability normalization")
    check(abs(enumerated_yield - yield_rate) < 1e-12, "enumerated yield")
    for i in range(len(orders)):
        check(abs(enumerated_s[i] - expected_s[i]) < 1e-12, "enumerated cost")
    check(0 < yield_rate <= 1, "positive yield for cost normalization")
    check(0 < saved_fraction < 1, "this ordering saves work")
    check(abs(swap_gain_s - (expected_s[1] - expected_s[0])) < 1e-12, "exchange gain equals cost difference")
    check(ratio_p < ratio_o, "order rule puts P before O")
    check(alt_ratio_p > ratio_o, "checkpoint variant reverses the order")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Computed Display Exports) ───────────────────────────
    n_str = fmt_int(n_rollouts)
    yield_str = fmt_percent(yield_rate, precision=2, style="prose")
    admitted_str = fmt_int(round(expected_admitted))
    savings_str = fmt_percent(saved_fraction, precision=1, style="prose")
    r_pass_str = fmt_percent(pass_rates[0], precision=0, style="symbol")
    u_pass_str = fmt_percent(pass_rates[1], precision=0, style="symbol")
    p_pass_str = fmt_percent(pass_rates[2], precision=0, style="symbol")
    o_pass_str = fmt_percent(pass_rates[3], precision=0, style="symbol")
    t_pass_str = fmt_percent(pass_rates[4], precision=0, style="symbol")
    r_cost_str = fmt_qty(costs_s[0] * second, second, precision=2)
    u_cost_str = fmt_qty(costs_s[1] * second, second, precision=2)
    p_cost_str = fmt_qty(costs_s[2] * second, second, precision=2)
    o_cost_str = fmt_qty(costs_s[3] * second, second, precision=0)
    t_cost_str = fmt_qty(costs_s[4] * second, second, precision=0)
    p_first_attempt_str = fmt_qty(expected_s[0] * second, second, precision=4)
    o_first_attempt_str = fmt_qty(expected_s[1] * second, second, precision=4)
    p_first_admitted_str = fmt_qty(expected_s[0] / yield_rate * second, second, precision=2)
    o_first_admitted_str = fmt_qty(expected_s[1] / yield_rate * second, second, precision=2)
    reach_po_str = fmt(reach_po, precision=3)
    p_pass_dec_str = fmt(pass_rates[2], precision=1)
    o_pass_dec_str = fmt(pass_rates[3], precision=1)
    ratio_p_str = fmt_qty(ratio_p * second, second, precision=0)
    ratio_o_str = fmt_qty(ratio_o * second, second, precision=1)
    ratio_t_str = fmt_qty(ratio_t * second, second, precision=0)
    swap_gain_str = fmt_qty(swap_gain_s * second, second, precision=2)
    alt_p_cost_str = fmt_qty(alt_p_cost_s * second, second, precision=0)
    alt_p_pass_str = fmt_percent(alt_p_pass, precision=0, style="prose")
    o_pass_prose_str = fmt_percent(pass_rates[3], precision=0, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-14-verification-cascade-economics-and-throughput .callout-notebook title="Admission ordering with the same accepted set"}

**Problem**: A batch of `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.n_str` candidate trajectory records enters an end-to-end demonstration admission route evaluated under predicates $\text{chk}_{\text{record}}, \text{chk}_{\text{use}}, \text{chk}_{\text{proc}}, \text{chk}_{\text{out}}, \text{chk}_{\text{target}}$. Record fidelity ($\text{chk}_{\text{record}}$) and permitted-use ($\text{chk}_{\text{use}}$) checks must execute first due to data dependencies. Target suitability ($\text{chk}_{\text{target}}$) executes last because its review reads the test artifacts that $\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$ produces. The process audit ($\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}$) and outcome verification ($\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$) can execute in either order. Which evaluation sequence minimizes verifier slot time, and how much total compute does it save?

**Variables**: Each predicate evaluation resolves deterministically to `pass` or `fail`. For this analysis, pass events are modeled as mutually independent, ensuring invariant marginal pass probabilities across permutations. Each reached verifier occupies a dedicated worker slot for the duration that @tbl-vol3-cascade-cost-inputs lists beside its pass probability. The trajectory record and candidate repository snapshot are immutable. Pre-execution authorization, container containment, and grader protections are enforced prior to running any test suites. Upstream rollout generation, job scheduling delays, candidate storage, and human review costs are excluded.

| Predicate                    | Hypothetical pass probability                                |                         Occupied slot time per reached check |
|:-----------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------:|
| $\text{chk}_{\text{record}}$ | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.r_pass_str` | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.r_cost_str` |
| $\text{chk}_{\text{use}}$    | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.u_pass_str` | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.u_cost_str` |
| $\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}$   | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.p_pass_str` | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.p_cost_str` |
| $\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$    | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.o_pass_str` | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.o_cost_str` |
| $\text{chk}_{\text{target}}$ | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.t_pass_str` | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.t_cost_str` |

: **Inputs for one hypothetical admission route**: Independence and fixed durations make order changes comparable without reusing incompatible conditional measurements. {#tbl-vol3-cascade-cost-inputs}

**Math**: Applying @eq-vol3-trajectory-curation-order-rule, the cost per rejection is `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.p_cost_str` / (1 − `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.p_pass_dec_str`) = `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.ratio_p_str` for process audit $\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}$, compared to `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.o_cost_str` / (1 − `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.o_pass_dec_str`) = `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.ratio_o_str` for outcome verification $\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$. Because $\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}$ yields rejections far more cost-effectively than $\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$, scheduling $\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}$ ahead of $\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$ minimizes expected compute. Both predicates are reached with joint probability `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.reach_po_str` (the product of pass rates for $\text{chk}_{\text{record}}$ and $\text{chk}_{\text{use}}$). Swapping the sequence saves $\RecordAdequacyPassProbability \PermittedUsePassProbability [\OutcomeCheckSlotTime(1-\ProcessConditionPassProbability) - \ProcessConditionCheckTime(1-\OutcomeCheckPassProbability)]$, yielding `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.swap_gain_str` saved per attempted record. Evaluating @eq-verifier-cost-cascade across the parameters in @tbl-vol3-cascade-cost-inputs produces the overall slot durations in @tbl-vol3-cascade-cost-results, verified through exhaustive state-space enumeration.

| Order                                                                                                                                        |                               Expected slot time per attempted record |                                 Expected slot time per admitted record |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------:|-----------------------------------------------------------------------:|
| $\text{chk}_{\text{record}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{use}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{proc}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{out}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{target}}$ | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.p_first_attempt_str` | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.p_first_admitted_str` |
| $\text{chk}_{\text{record}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{use}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{out}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{proc}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{target}}$ | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.o_first_attempt_str` | `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.o_first_admitted_str` |

: **Equal-criterion ordering comparison**: Both orders stop this route at its first failure. Other uses of rejected records require separate work accounting. {#tbl-vol3-cascade-cost-results}

**Result**: Both schedules in @tbl-vol3-cascade-cost-results achieve an identical expected yield of `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.yield_str`, admitting approximately `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.admitted_str` valid demonstrations from the batch. Evaluating process compliance $\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}$ prior to sandbox testing $\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$ reduces total verifier slot time by `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.savings_str`, without discarding a single valid trajectory or lowering any quality threshold.

**Systems insight**: Sequence independent, fixed-cost admission verifiers within permissible orders by cost per rejection, $\CheckSlotTime_i / (1 - \CheckPassProbability_i)$, rather than by raw duration alone. Ordering by cost per rejection places fast, selective filters ahead of expensive, permissive verifiers while guaranteeing an identical admitted set. These compute savings require neither cutting validation corners nor loosening thresholds. The dependency fixed in the problem is what keeps target suitability $\text{chk}_{\text{target}}$ last here. Its cost per rejection is `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.ratio_t_str`, below the outcome check's `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.ratio_o_str`, so a target review that did not read the test artifacts would belong ahead of $\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$ as well. Data dependencies, container cold-start amortization, and compliance boundaries constrain permissible schedules. Correlated checks require comparing admissible orders with measured conditional pass rates and reached-check costs in @eq-verifier-cost-cascade.

:::

### Learned scores and scoped judgments {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-rankers}

Deterministic checks cannot score open-ended prose quality or step-by-step reasoning clarity, yet letting a learned scorer or brevity filter admit trajectories on its own either admits flawed runs that game the scorer or strips out the multi-turn recovery paths the policy needs to learn error correction. Learned scoring models are still useful for ranking candidate trajectories for manual review or sub-sampling from a pool of verified examples to balance diversity and conciseness. Process reward models, for instance, score individual reasoning steps and intermediate tool calls rather than only final task outcomes [@uesato2022solving; @lightman2023let]. Even so, a low step score only flags a likely point of failure; pinpointing the root cause still requires human or symbolic review.

When tasks require evaluating open-ended prose, user interactions, or design quality, human raters or judge models supply scores governed by explicit rubrics and calibration standards. The verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) bounds what such a score can do inside a cascade. A learned assessment can rank candidates or supply scoped evidence for one qualitative criterion, but it is not an independent guarantee. When valid records are rare, even a small false-accept rate fills the admitted set with invalid ones. The judge's input must therefore be limited to the evidence its criterion names and kept away from anything the candidate wrote to influence its grader. Deterministic verifiers require the same scoping: every verifier execution records the assessor version, rubric hash, extracted evidence, confidence scores, and explicit abstentions, and a high qualitative rating never overrides a failed deterministic check.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Qualitative rubrics and grader calibration standards are established in @sec-vol3-evaluation-grading-calibration.
:::

Repeated selection against an automated scorer also concentrates the scorer's blind spots. Filtering training data against a learned proxy score initially improves output quality, but continued optimization eventually triggers proxy collapse, where the proxy score keeps rising while true downstream task quality falls [@gao2023scaling]. This is the same divergence that best-of-N selection produces against an imperfect check at inference time (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-pressure), except that curation writes the winners into the next policy's weights. Mitigating this feedback loop requires periodic double-blind audits of both accepted and rejected records, continuous recalibration against held-out ground truth that never enters training, and re-scoring whenever policy architectures or task domains shift. Any data augmentation or trajectory transformation likewise requires fresh verification of its modified payload and token masks, a provenance boundary that @sec-vol3-flywheel-provenance develops.

::: {#chk-14-admission-cascades-limits .callout-checkpoint title="Defend an admission route"}

A route is defensible when each predicate's verdict and the order of checking can both be justified.

**Deciding admission**

- [ ] **Record vs. target**: A collection trace faithfully records a malformed proposal rejected before dispatch and a later correction. Why can $\text{chk}_{\text{record}}$ pass without making the malformed proposal an imitation target?
- [ ] **Incomplete outcome**: A new collection run has only a targeted pass for its candidate under `repair_accept_v1`. Decide which route it can enter now, and name the evidence the full demonstration route still needs.
- [ ] **Consumer choice**: What additional evidence turns a stored negative into a preference comparison, and what separate artifact supports fresh reward-scored rollouts?

**Pricing the cascade**

- [ ] **Order estimate**: Retaining the notebook's independence and fixed-duration premises, suppose the process audit $\text{chk}_{\text{proc}}$ instead costs `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.alt_p_cost_str` and passes `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.alt_p_pass_str` of records, with $\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$ unchanged at `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.o_cost_str` and `{python} VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.o_pass_prose_str`. Compute each predicate's cost per rejection and decide which runs first.
- [ ] **Grader boundary**: Which of the three tamper mechanisms would have caught the tampered reproducer in @lst-vol3-curation-assert-true, and why is a read-only test file alone insufficient?

:::

By evaluating trajectories through staged, consumer-specific cascades rather than forcing all data through a single cleanliness filter, the curation pipeline produces verified datasets tailored to distinct imitation, preference, and rollout objectives. Verifying clean executions, however, leaves the harder half of the data problem unsolved: production agents encounter disruptions, and training a policy to recover requires curating traces that contain mistakes without teaching the model to repeat them.

## Recovery Demonstration Curation {#sec-vol3-flywheel-curation}

When an agent issues a malformed tool call, receives a rejection from the environment runtime, and then inspects the schema to produce a passing patch, its trace records both a mistake and a valid repair. A naive curation pipeline might discard this trace because it contains a failed step, or edit out the error to make the agent appear infallible. Either choice discards the evidence of how to recover from an imperfect prefix. Admitting the successful repair while keeping the original misstep as conditioning context requires deciding which recovery trajectories to harvest, how to mask them safely, and how much training capacity to give them.

A training corpus composed solely of error-free trajectories teaches an agent how to act only when every prior step succeeded. In production, however, noisy tool outputs, transient network faults, and early mistakes push an agent off the nominal path. Once off that path, a model trained only on clean prefixes faces states it never saw during training, and over a long horizon a recoverable detour turns into a failed task. This distribution mismatch[^fn-compounding-imitation-error] creates the need for recovery demonstrations, and the curation pipeline's job is to capture, validate, and package those recovery episodes with their conditioning evidence intact.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Exposure bias, the mismatch between training on recorded prefixes and running on prefixes the policy produced itself, and its horizon-dependent cost are developed in @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-exposure-bias.
:::

[^fn-compounding-imitation-error]: **Compounding Imitation Error**: A policy trained only on states visited by an expert can turn a per-step error rate $\PerStepErrorRate$ (the per-step error rate of horizon compounding, @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding) into as many as $\TurnHorizon^2\PerStepErrorRate$ mistakes over an $\TurnHorizon$-step task, because an early error exposes the policy to states absent from its training distribution. Querying an expert interactively on learner-visited states, the core mechanism of DAgger, restores an error bound that grows linearly in $\TurnHorizon$ [@ross2011reduction]. Recovery demonstrations are the offline curation counterpart: they supply supervised repair targets on the flawed state prefixes that direct-success collection omits. \index{Imitation learning!compounding error}

::: {#dfn-recovery-demonstration .callout-definition title="Recovery demonstration"}

A ***recovery demonstration***\index{Recovery demonstration!definition} is a curated trajectory record or isolated sequence segment that pairs the context of an operational disruption (a model mistake, environment fault, or partial observation) with an action assessed as correct under the task specification and runtime authority boundaries.

1. **Significance**: Recovery demonstrations directly address long-horizon execution stability. Under horizon compounding (@eq-vol3-horizon-compounding), any step-level error that the policy can successfully remediate becomes a temporary detour rather than an irrecoverable task failure. Direct-success harvesting systematically starves the training distribution of these pivotal recovery branches.
2. **Distinction**: An appropriate recovery action depends on context: it may diagnose an exception, retry with corrected parameters, back off, or hand off control to a human supervisor. It does not require the agent to overcome an outage it cannot repair or to exceed its authority to finish the task.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating every token in an eventually successful trajectory as a positive imitation target, thereby inadvertently teaching the model to repeat the initial mistake.

:::

### Record roles and learning uses {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-record-roles}

A single extended trajectory may begin with clean progress, hit an unexpected environment error, execute a sound recovery, and later stall on an unrelated tool failure. Discarding that entire trajectory wastes genuine recovery signal, whereas training uncritically on all of its tokens teaches the model to replicate its bugs. Because a trace rarely fits a single outcome bucket, labels such as direct success, recovery, and negative describe the behavioral evidence a segment contains rather than granting blanket permission for training. The predicates of @tbl-vol3-verifier-cascade-stages already separate the two decisions. Record adequacy and permitted use are shared across routes, while the process, outcome, and target predicates are set by the consumer. A role label therefore indicates which consumer-specific checks a segment might pass (@tbl-vol3-trajectory-taxonomy).

| Record role                  | Evidence worth preserving                                                                   | Learning-use decision                                                                                                                              |
|:-----------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Direct-success demonstration | Grounded actions and adequate evidence for the declared result                              | Select useful responses under the demonstration policy; shortest length and absence of error codes are not sufficient criteria                     |
| Recovery demonstration       | The preceding context, observed disruption, response, and evidence for its assessed outcome | Select the justified response while retaining the mistake or fault as context where needed                                                         |
| Hard-negative candidate      | A plausible but inadequate response, with evidence identifying the relevant deficiency      | Consider diagnostic use, a separately assessed segment, or a compatible preference comparison; do not automatically imitate the deficient response |

: **Behavioral Roles and Learning Uses**: Record labels describe evidence. Each intended consumer still requires its own admission conditions. {#tbl-vol3-trajectory-taxonomy}

A **hard negative**\index{Hard negative!definition} is an action or plan that looks plausible under surface checks, such as valid syntax, expected keywords, or a passing local smoke test, yet fails full functional verification. Pinpointing the exact step where an agentic trace went wrong is rarely simple. A failed assertion at the end of a run confirms that an error occurred without naming the earlier decision that caused it. Repeated tool calls that look like a loop may be legitimate polling against an asynchronous job. Curation systems therefore record the failure signal that implicates a candidate divergence step together with an explicit note when the first causal step is uncertain, rather than inventing an exact divergence point. Engineering teams also frequently assume that any recorded negative can be paired immediately with a success to train a preference objective, or replayed as a baseline for reinforcement learning against a verifiable reward. Both shortcuts fail in practice. A negative forms a valid comparison only under the shared-context condition of @sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-learning-artifacts, which a success generated under a different prompt, an extra hint, or updated tool outputs violates. A reinforcement learning baseline, in turn, needs a live, resettable fixture rather than a stored failure transcript.

::: {#psp-14-hard-negative-hazard .callout-perspective title="A recorded mistake is context, not a target"}

A pervasive misconception in trajectory engineering is that an imitation training set must consist exclusively of pristine, error-free transcripts. In reality, a curated training dataset consists of complete conversational contexts coupled with explicit target masks, and these two components serve fundamentally different purposes.

A flawed model response should receive no direct positive imitation target loss. Nevertheless, that erroneous response must remain in the prompt history if subsequent recovery actions are to make any sense; a correction is meaningful only in the context of the error it resolves. Conversely, an execution trace that ultimately timed out or failed an integration test often contains early sub-tasks solved with exemplary precision. The curation pipeline marks which spans represent valid targets and which represent conditioning context; the loss-masking subsystem then omits their direct next-token loss terms while retaining them as conditioning during fine-tuning. Masking errors out of the loss while retaining them in the attention context teaches the model how to react to a failure without training it to generate one.

:::

### Conditioning evidence for a correction {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-conditioning-evidence}

In collection run `collection_run_r19_01`, target selection separates context from targets on task `pool_repair_01` inside test environment `pool_fixture_v1`. The run produces workspace candidate `ws_r20` and captures raw trace `trace_r19_01` (workspace numbers count candidate revisions after the evaluation trial's `ws_r19`, while run and trace numbers count collection batches). End-to-end grading confirms that `ws_r20` satisfies `repair_accept_v1`, meeting all process constraints, resource ceilings, and cleanup duties.

The run belongs to a campaign whose declared learning use is recovery from harness refusals. Unlike the truncated observation that opened the chapter, this behavior is collected on the premise, recorded in the collection manifest, that the ladder's probes left it with the model. Supplying the schema in context and validating proposals against a strict schema still left the policy emitting malformed edits that the runtime had to refuse. What remains to teach is how to respond after a refusal, and the recorded event sequence shows how that recovery unfolds:

- Event `e1` delivers the task prompt, tool definitions, and repository context.
- At event `e2`, the model proposes a file edit with a malformed argument. Because the tool runtime validates inputs locally before dispatch, it refuses the call immediately, and the trace records the refusal without logging an applied write.
- At event `e3`, the model reads the refusal, requests the API schema documentation, and inspects the returned specification.
- At event `e4`, the model issues a corrected, schema-compliant edit, and the tool enforces an atomic version check alongside the update rather than relying on a stale earlier read.
- At event `e5`, the harness runs the required checks on the edited workspace and returns their summary as an observation.
- At event `e6`, the model summarizes the validated changes, states the patch scope, and closes the session.

Under curation policy `repair_accept_v1`, an initial syntax refusal that the agent diagnoses and corrects promptly is eligible for recovery training. A target-selection manifest marks the actions worth imitating without editing the recorded sequence of events:

```json
{
  "collection_run_id": "collection_run_r19_01",
  "source_trace_id": "trace_r19_01",
  "criteria_version": "repair_accept_v1",
  "target_selection_version": "recovery_targets_v1",
  "behavioral_role": "recovery",
  "context_only_events": ["e2", "e5"],
  "selected_response_events": ["e3", "e4", "e6"],
  "assessment_scope": "recorded correction and supported final report"
}
```

The source trace preserves the original task prompt, tool definitions, intermediate observations, and evaluation logs intact, while target selection marks only the policy tokens inside events `e3`, `e4`, and `e6`. The refused proposal (`e2`) and test summary (`e5`) stay in the sequence as conditioning context, supplying the history that makes the schema lookup and corrected edit make sense. Passing the overall task does not make every intermediate action a training target; each selected step must be a sound decision given what the agent knew at that turn. Placed beside the other two record roles, the recovery record sits between a direct success, whose supported responses can all be targets, and a hard negative, whose deficient response is never one (@fig-vol3-trajectory-typology).

::: {#fig-vol3-trajectory-typology fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Record Roles and Selected Targets**: Each role is drawn as a sequence of events, with selected targets distinguished from context. In the recovery demonstration, the refused malformed proposal at e2 and the check summary at e5 stay as context while e3, e4, and e6 become targets. A hard-negative candidate looks adequate under a targeted check and fails a required one. Its deficient response is never an imitation target, and where it went wrong is recorded with its basis rather than fixed at an exact step." fig-alt="Three horizontal lanes of event tiles ordered left to right, each with a loss mask strip beneath the tiles. Direct-success demonstration: task and delivered context, inspect the failing check, edit the pool wakeup, required checks pass, report the supported result, with the second, third, and fifth tiles shaded blue as targets. Recovery demonstration: earlier context and observations, then e2 malformed edit refused with a red dashed border, e3 inspect the schema, e4 corrected permitted edit, e5 check summary, and e6 report result and scope, with e3, e4, and e6 shaded blue as targets. Hard-negative candidate: task and delivered context, plausible edit with a red dashed border, targeted check passes, required check fails, with no targets; a dotted red bracket under the last three tiles reads first causal step uncertain: basis recorded. Mask strip segments are blue under target tiles and light gray elsewhere. A legend identifies selected target, context or observation, deficient never imitated, and in loss mask."}
![](images/svg/vol3-trajectory-typology.svg)
:::

When only a local recovery window has verified evidence, the curation harness can admit that segment alone while leaving the broader task outcome marked as unverified. Likewise, if post-processing scrubs credentials or private paths to create `trace_r19_01_redacted_v1`, the pipeline must re-verify the target spans against the modified tokens. Deleting the malformed call, pasting future test outputs into an earlier prompt, or truncating intermediate observations changes the causal problem the model is being asked to learn. Preserving those causal links inside harvested traces is only half of recovery curation, however, because waiting passively for natural failures leaves rare fault modes unrepresented.

### Fault injection {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-fault-injection}

In production, routine execution occasionally exposes an agent to network drops, service timeouts, and tool errors, but waiting for spontaneous failures leaves wide gaps in the training corpus. Systematic **fault injection**\index{Fault injection!recovery collection}[^fn-fault-injection-chaos] fills those gaps deliberately. A collection protocol logs the injection version, the targeted tool call or observation stream, the simulated system state, and the expected recovery action. Fault injection stays strictly inside the runtime's security boundaries: injecting a network timeout or file lock grants the agent no extra authority to install unapproved packages, widen filesystem permissions, or bypass human approval gates. Each condition in @tbl-vol3-fault-injection-taxonomy names the causal distinction the fixture must preserve and the response a curator checks.

[^fn-fault-injection-chaos]: **Fault Injection**: Introducing controlled failures to test resilience is a classic systems practice, popularized in distributed infrastructure as chaos engineering, which injects server, network, and disk faults into live clusters to check steady-state behavior [@basiri2016]. Curation borrows the experimental discipline rather than the live production venue: faults are injected inside versioned, hermetic test fixtures where every fault is logged and environment state transitions stay deterministic, so demonstrations teach genuine recovery rather than quirks of the simulator. \index{Fault injection!chaos engineering}

| Collection condition                               | Required causal distinction                                    | Candidate response to assess                                   |
|:---------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|
| Malformed proposal rejected locally                | No operation was dispatched                                    | Inspect the schema and correct the represented error           |
| Partial search result                              | Missing content is distinguished from an empty complete result | Request a valid continuation or report insufficient evidence   |
| Lost acknowledgment after a state-changing request | The endpoint may have acted despite the missing reply          | Reconcile the identified operation before a dependent retry    |
| Unavailable capability or exhausted allowance      | The original goal may be unreachable within the grant          | Stop or hand off with accurate scope and owned residual duties |

: **Fault Conditions for Recovery Collection**: Each condition preserves the relation between observations and possible effects. The criterion evaluates an appropriate response, not compulsory autonomous repair. {#tbl-vol3-fault-injection-taxonomy}

Consider the lost-acknowledgment case in @tbl-vol3-fault-injection-taxonomy. When a mock harness drops an acknowledgment after committing a state-changing remote call, the simulated environment must keep the side effects of that committed call in its state. If the mock returned a connection reset while silently rolling the server state back to a clean slate, it would misrepresent the distributed systems hazard and train the agent to retry blindly, causing duplicate writes in production. Replay determinism requires that every subsequent observation reflect the mutations that actually occurred.

Engineering teams must also separate tasks meant to teach autonomous repair from tasks meant to teach safe stopping. A recovery task provides an authorized, reachable fix inside the test environment; a safe-stopping task deliberately closes every repair path so the agent learns to halt cleanly and hand off to an operator. Because the two objectives require different grading rubrics, reliability coverage tracks unprompted agent mistakes and injected faults separately while recording any production failure modes that the fixture cannot reproduce. Harvesting these multi-turn recovery traces, however, changes the token geometry of the resulting corpus.

### Records, stored tokens, and selected targets {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-token-accounting}

Because a recovery trajectory includes diagnostic cycles, failed attempts, and error observations, it is much longer than a direct-success run, yet only the corrected responses carry supervised loss. As a result, the share of recovery trajectories in a corpus matches neither their share of stored tokens on disk nor their share of active target tokens during training. Curation accounting starts from a retained pool of trajectories and draws subsets for specific training artifacts. One retained trace may supply conditioning context and target spans to an imitation corpus while also entering a preference pair, yet it remains a single task execution in the pool.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_trajectory_curation_margin_003.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three horizontal bars showing the recovery class's share of the hypothetical pool under three denominators: 25 percent of records, 45 percent of stored tokens, and 39 percent of selected target tokens."}

*One recovery class, three shares: records, stored tokens, targets.*
:::

For a trajectory category $\TrajectoryCategoryIndex$, let $\CategoryRecordCount_j$ denote the number of retained records, $\MeanStoredTokensPerRecord^{(\TrajectoryCategoryIndex)}$ denote the average stored tokens per record under the active tokenizer, and $\MeanTargetTokensPerRecord_j$ denote the average selected target tokens per record admitted into a specific imitation fine-tuning artifact. The total stored token volume $\StoredTokenVolume_j$ and total target token volume $\TargetTokenVolume_j$ are:

$$\StoredTokenVolume_j=\CategoryRecordCount_j\MeanStoredTokensPerRecord^{(\TrajectoryCategoryIndex)},\qquad \TargetTokenVolume_j=\CategoryRecordCount_j\MeanTargetTokensPerRecord_j.$$

The stored token share measures $\StoredTokenVolume_j$ against the total tokens in the repository, whereas the target token share measures $\TargetTokenVolume_j$ against the active supervised tokens in the training dataset. Confusing the two breaks capacity planning. Processed tokens (context plus targets) drive attention compute and memory traffic during forward and backward passes. Selected target tokens, by contrast, decide which positions contribute direct loss terms (whose gradients still flow back through the conditioning context). Specifying a dataset mixture by record count while budgeting accelerators by target tokens, or vice versa, creates scheduling surprises, especially when multi-turn conversations are unrolled without prefix sharing.

```{python}
#| label: lego-14-sizing-and-token-budget-allocation
#| echo: false
# CORPUS DENOMINATORS (LEGO)
# Goal: Separate retained records, stored context, and selected imitation targets.
# Scope: Hypothetical disjoint role counts; one emitted sequence per demo record.
from mlsysim import Scenarios
from mlsysim.core.units import token
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent

class MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation:
    # 1. LOAD: stipulated retained-pool counts and tokenizer-specific means (scenario).
    scenario = Scenarios.RecoveryPoolDenominators
    n_direct, l_direct, u_direct = scenario.classes["direct"]
    n_recover, l_recover, u_recover = scenario.classes["recovery"]
    n_negative, l_negative, _ = scenario.classes["negative"]

    # 2. EXECUTE: this artifact admits direct/recovery records, not negatives.
    pool = scenario.result
    n_total = pool.records
    n_demo = n_direct + n_recover
    v_direct, v_recover, v_negative = n_direct * l_direct, n_recover * l_recover, n_negative * l_negative
    v_total = pool.stored_tokens
    v_demo = pool.admitted_stored_tokens
    u_total = pool.target_tokens
    count_share = pool.record_share
    stored_share = pool.stored_share
    demo_context_share = pool.admitted_stored_share
    target_share = pool.target_share
    ctx_per_target_direct = pool.context_per_target["direct"]
    ctx_per_target_recover = pool.context_per_target["recovery"]

    # 3. GUARD: named denominators, logical-token totals, and target bounds.
    check(n_total == 50_000 and n_demo == 45_000, "Separate retained and demo counts")
    check(v_total.to(token).magnitude == 514_250_000, "Retained logical tokens")
    check(v_demo.to(token).magnitude == 465_250_000, "Demo logical tokens")
    check(u_total.to(token).magnitude == 64_000_000, "Selected target tokens")
    check(0 < u_direct <= l_direct and 0 < u_recover <= l_recover, "Targets within records")
    check(abs(count_share - 0.25) < 1e-12, "Count share")
    check(abs(stored_share - 0.4496840058) < 1e-9, "Stored share")
    check(abs(demo_context_share - 0.4970445997) < 1e-9, "Demo context share")
    check(abs(target_share - 0.390625) < 1e-12, "Target share")

    # 4. OUTPUT: every export is consumed in the worksheet below.
    n_total_str, n_demo_str = fmt_int(n_total), fmt_int(n_demo)
    n_direct_str, n_recover_str, n_negative_str = fmt_int(n_direct), fmt_int(n_recover), fmt_int(n_negative)
    l_direct_str = fmt_int(l_direct.to(token).magnitude)
    l_recover_str = fmt_int(l_recover.to(token).magnitude)
    l_negative_str = fmt_int(l_negative.to(token).magnitude)
    u_direct_str = fmt_int(u_direct.to(token).magnitude)
    u_recover_str = fmt_int(u_recover.to(token).magnitude)
    v_total_str = fmt_int(v_total.to(token).magnitude)
    v_demo_str = fmt_int(v_demo.to(token).magnitude)
    u_total_str = fmt_int(u_total.to(token).magnitude)
    count_share_str = fmt_percent(count_share, precision=0, style="prose")
    stored_share_str = fmt_percent(stored_share, precision=2, style="prose")
    demo_context_share_str = fmt_percent(demo_context_share, precision=2, style="prose")
    target_share_str = fmt_percent(target_share, precision=2, style="prose")
    v_direct_str = fmt_int(v_direct.to(token).magnitude)
    v_recover_str = fmt_int(v_recover.to(token).magnitude)
    v_negative_str = fmt_int(v_negative.to(token).magnitude)
    u_direct_total_str = fmt_int((n_direct * u_direct).to(token).magnitude)
    u_recover_total_str = fmt_int((n_recover * u_recover).to(token).magnitude)
    ctx_direct_str = fmt(ctx_per_target_direct, precision=0)
    ctx_recover_str = fmt(ctx_per_target_recover, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-14-sizing-and-token-budget-allocation .callout-notebook title="One pool, three different token allocations"}

**Problem**: Consider a hypothetical retained corpus containing `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.n_total_str` records categorized into disjoint roles. The demonstration policy admits direct successes and recovery trajectories; negative trajectories are reserved for diagnostic logging and preference modeling, providing zero imitation targets for this artifact. Using the empirical means listed in @tbl-vol3-curation-token-allocation, determine the fractional share that recovery trajectories occupy across three distinct denominators: total records, tokens (stored in the repository and processed by this artifact), and supervised target tokens.

| Retained class |                                                      Records |                                Mean stored tokens per record |                      Mean selected target tokens per record |
|:---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------:|-------------------------------------------------------------:|------------------------------------------------------------:|
| Direct         |   `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.n_direct_str` |   `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.l_direct_str` |  `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.u_direct_str` |
| Recovery       |  `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.n_recover_str` |  `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.l_recover_str` | `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.u_recover_str` |
| Negative       | `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.n_negative_str` | `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.l_negative_str` |                             None in this imitation artifact |

: **Inputs to the Corpus Allocation Worksheet**: Counts and lengths are hypothetical, not an empirically recommended mixture. Selected targets refer to one presentation of each eligible record under a fixed tokenizer and selection policy. {#tbl-vol3-curation-token-allocation}

**Math**: Total stored tokens follow $\StoredTokenVolume_j = \CategoryRecordCount_j\MeanStoredTokensPerRecord^{(\TrajectoryCategoryIndex)}$: direct successes account for `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.v_direct_str`, recovery traces account for `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.v_recover_str`, and negatives account for `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.v_negative_str`, totaling `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.v_total_str` across the repository and `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.v_demo_str` across admitted demonstration records. Supervised target tokens follow $\TargetTokenVolume_j = \CategoryRecordCount_j\MeanTargetTokensPerRecord_j$: direct demonstrations contribute `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.u_direct_total_str` target tokens and recovery traces contribute `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.u_recover_total_str` target tokens, totaling `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.u_total_str` supervisory tokens.

**Result**: Recovery accounts for `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.count_share_str` of total retained records, `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.stored_share_str` of all stored tokens in the repository, `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.demo_context_share_str` of the admitted demonstration tokens, and `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.target_share_str` of active target supervision tokens. The two token shares answer different questions. The repository share includes negatives that this artifact never trains on, so it prices storage; the admitted-demonstration share counts the tokens that training actually processes, so it prices compute.

**Systems insight**: Always formulate training mixtures in terms of target tokens while budgeting accelerator compute and memory in terms of processed context tokens. The operational multiplier separating these two metrics is the context-to-target ratio: `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.ctx_recover_str` stored context tokens per target token for recovery traces, compared to `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.ctx_direct_str` for direct successes. Increasing the recovery proportion inflates processed context volume far faster than supervised gradient signal. An engineering team that configures a mixture purely by record count will request a `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.count_share_str` recovery ratio but will end up committing `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.stored_share_str` of repository storage and `{python} MixedCurationTokenBudgetAllocation.demo_context_share_str` of processed training tokens to recovery records. Naive multi-turn serialization that repeatedly unrolls conversational prefixes amplifies this computational overhead even further.

:::

### Mixture experiments {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-mixture-experiments}

Token accounting prices the storage and compute footprint of a recovery-heavy corpus, but it cannot tell whether adding more recovery traces actually improves fault tolerance or crowds out direct-path competence on routine tasks. Answering that question requires an empirical mixture experiment that holds the evaluation protocol, base checkpoint, target-masking rules, and training schedule fixed while varying the recovery ratio across training cohorts. Curation engineers track deduplication and replacement in each cohort, because raising the recovery share under a fixed training budget reduces coverage of direct-path tasks.

Because context-to-target ratios differ by role, an experiment must state which denominator it holds constant and report results under both. Fixing total supervised target tokens forces the recovery-heavy cohort to process far more conditioning context tokens, raising training wall-clock time and FLOPs; fixing total processed tokens gives the recovery-heavy cohort fewer supervised target updates. When accelerator hours or training windows are hard limits, teams compare candidate mixtures at equal wall-clock time or compute cost. They screen those candidates on the development split and test the chosen configuration once on the held-out evaluation benchmark. To keep aggregate scores from hiding regressions, evaluation reports break results down across nominal tasks, injected fault conditions, and out-of-distribution transfer suites before computing any summary metric. They track task acceptance alongside hallucinated tool outputs, redundant steps, clean stops, and total token spend.

Once an effective mixture is chosen, its parameters are written into the **corpus manifest**\index{Corpus manifest!definition}, the machine-readable, versioned record that publishes a corpus and tells a trainer what each member is and how it may be used.[^fn-datasheet-manifest-curation] Beyond the mixture weights, the manifest binds input trajectory pool identifiers, selection filter versions, token accounting denominators, test coverage matrices, and audit logs, whose per-record lineage and publication are developed in @sec-vol3-flywheel-provenance and @sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-manifest-publication. Deploying a model trained on this manifest changes the trajectories that subsequent collection runs produce. New failure modes and recoveries feed back into the harvesting pipeline, which closes a loop in which the policy being improved also generates the data that improves it.

[^fn-datasheet-manifest-curation]: **Dataset Documentation**: Documenting datasets with structured records that state how they were built, what they contain, and what uses they support was proposed by analogy to hardware datasheets in electronics [@gebru2021]. A corpus manifest turns that documentation into a machine-checked contract for agent pipelines: its fields bind cryptographically to dataset versions, filter code, and verification logs so that training jobs can check corpus invariants automatically before starting a run. \index{Corpus manifest!datasheet lineage}

## The Self-Improvement Loop {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-self-improvement}

Suppose a curation round for the connection-pool repair agent retains only straight-line, clean executions while discarding messier traces where the agent recovers from misleading test diagnostics. Fine-tuning on that corpus strengthens straightforward repairs while leaving recovery unimproved, and in the next round a higher nominal pass rate hides that gap rather than closing it. Because corpus selection shapes the behaviors the next policy generation learns and samples, curators track three distinct signals in every round: what the current policy sampled, what the curation cascade kept, and how the resulting model scores under independent held-out evaluation.

### Rejection-sampling fine-tuning {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-rejection-sampling}

When a team lacks human demonstrations for new task fixtures, it can bootstrap training data from the current policy whenever verifying a candidate solution is easier than generating one, provided it logs attempted, rejected, and unverified runs alongside retained examples so a looser filter is never mistaken for a better model. In this generate–select–train loop, a versioned policy samples executions across a suite of task fixtures within a fixed compute budget. The admission cascade routes the resulting traces by role: clean demonstrations feed imitation buffers, branched pairs populate preference datasets, and unresolved traces enter diagnostic storage. Training on the admitted records produces a candidate checkpoint, which held-out evaluation tests to decide whether it becomes the generator for the next collection round (an internal development promotion that stays separate from production release).

Selecting sampled successes for imitation is **rejection-sampling fine-tuning**\index{Rejection-sampling fine-tuning!definition}.[^fn-expert-iteration-curation] The Self-Taught Reasoner (STaR) illustrates this loop in bootstrapped reasoning. The model generates candidate rationales, keeps those that reach correct answers, fine-tunes on them, and uses ground-truth answers to prompt new rationales on tasks it initially failed [@zelikman2022star]. In agentic tasks, an automated verifier checks that a run satisfies its acceptance criteria, while target review still checks that the intermediate tool calls and state transitions are sound enough to imitate.

[^fn-expert-iteration-curation]: **Expert Iteration**: The generate–select–train loop predates language models. In expert iteration, tree search guided by the current network finds stronger moves than the network alone, the network is trained to imitate them, and the updated network guides the next round of search [@anthony2017thinking]. Rejection-sampling fine-tuning replaces tree search with repeated sampling and the expert with an automated check, which is why any blind spot in the check quickly becomes a habit of the loop. \index{Expert iteration!generate-select-train loop}

Different learning objectives need different outcome mixes across attempts on a fixture. An all-success batch supplies valid imitation demonstrations showing clean paths through tools. An all-failure batch yields no end-to-end demonstrations under a success filter, yet still supplies localized recovery segments, negative candidates for preference pairs, and failure traces for new regression fixtures. Group-relative training objectives, by contrast, require outcome variation within the same fixture. They score each rollout by its reward minus the mean reward of the rollouts sampled for that fixture, so a batch in which every rollout gets the same reward produces zero advantage on every rollout and contributes no reward-surrogate gradient.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Group relative policy optimization, which scores each rollout against the other rollouts sampled for the same task, is developed in @sec-vol3-rlvr-grpo.
:::

The sampling budget required to harvest these different data types follows from the per-attempt pass rate. Suppose the collection policy succeeds on a fixture with probability $\AttemptPassProbability$ per attempt, with each of the $\IndependentAttemptCount$ attempts executed independently. A simple success filter extracts a demonstration from the fixture if at least one attempt succeeds, an event that occurs with probability $1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount$. This expected yield sets the baseline compute cost per retained trajectory when the collector keeps at most one success from each full batch. For preference comparisons based on binary task acceptance and group-relative objectives with binary rewards, useful within-group contrast requires at least one success and at least one failure. Subtracting both the all-failure probability $(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount$ and the all-success probability $\AttemptPassProbability^{\IndependentAttemptCount}$ yields the **informative-task fraction**\index{Informative-task fraction!definition}:

$$\InformativeTaskFraction(\AttemptPassProbability,\IndependentAttemptCount)=1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount-\AttemptPassProbability^{\IndependentAttemptCount}.$$ {#eq-vol3-trajectory-curation-informative}

```{python}
#| label: lego-14-informative-task-fraction
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SUCCESS YIELD AND INFORMATIVE-TASK FRACTION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-trajectory-curation-informative.
# │ Goal: Show how per-attempt pass rate sets harvest yield and group contrast.
# │ Show: 1-(1-p)^k and 1-(1-p)^k-p^k at three pass rates for k attempts.
# │ How: Independent attempts with a fixed per-attempt pass probability.
# │ Note: Pass rates are illustrative, not measured fixture difficulties.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Scenarios
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent

class InformativeTaskFraction:
    # 1. LOAD: attempts per fixture and three illustrative pass rates (scenario).
    scenario = Scenarios.EightAttemptGroupContrast
    k = scenario.attempts
    p_low, p_mid, p_high = scenario.pass_rates

    # 2. EXECUTE: at least one success, then at least one of each outcome.
    yield_low = scenario.success_yield(p_low)
    yield_mid = scenario.success_yield(p_mid)
    yield_high = scenario.success_yield(p_high)
    mixed_low = scenario.mixed_fraction(p_low)
    mixed_mid = scenario.mixed_fraction(p_mid)
    mixed_high = scenario.mixed_fraction(p_high)
    attempts_low = scenario.attempts_per_success(p_low)

    # 3. GUARD: symmetry of the mixed fraction and the displayed scales.
    check(abs(mixed_low - mixed_high) < 1e-12, "Mixed fraction is symmetric in p and 1-p")
    check(0.33 < mixed_low < 0.34, "Low pass-rate mixed fraction")
    check(mixed_mid > 0.99, "Mid pass-rate mixed fraction")
    check(yield_high > 0.999, "High pass-rate yield is near one")
    check(23 < attempts_low < 24, "Attempts per harvested hard fixture")

    # 4. OUTPUT: every export is consumed in the paragraph below.
    k_str = fmt_int(k)
    low_str = fmt_percent(p_low, precision=0, style="prose")
    mid_str = fmt_percent(p_mid, precision=0, style="prose")
    high_str = fmt_percent(p_high, precision=0, style="prose")
    low_yield_str = fmt(yield_low, precision=2)
    low_mixed_str = fmt(mixed_low, precision=2)
    mid_mixed_str = fmt(mixed_mid, precision=2)
    high_mixed_str = fmt(mixed_high, precision=2)
    attempts_low_str = fmt_int(round(attempts_low))
```

With `{python} InformativeTaskFraction.k_str` attempts, a fixture the policy solves `{python} InformativeTaskFraction.low_str` of the time yields a success with probability only `{python} InformativeTaskFraction.low_yield_str`, requiring an average of about `{python} InformativeTaskFraction.attempts_low_str` attempts to harvest a single successful trajectory. That same fixture forms a mixed group of successes and failures with probability `{python} InformativeTaskFraction.low_mixed_str`.
