At `{python} InformativeTaskFraction.mid_str`, where the task is moderately difficult, the mixed fraction reaches `{python} InformativeTaskFraction.mid_mixed_str`, providing abundant pairwise contrast. When the pass rate reaches `{python} InformativeTaskFraction.high_str`, nearly every fixture yields a success, but the mixed fraction drops back to `{python} InformativeTaskFraction.high_mixed_str` because batches rarely include a failing attempt. @Eq-vol3-trajectory-curation-informative measures contrast rather than general utility. All-success groups remain valid demonstrations for imitation learning. By contrast, @sec-vol3-rlvr-grpo-zero-variance applies the $\AttemptPassProbability^{\IndependentAttemptCount}$ and $(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount$ terms to isolate groups whose uniform rewards offer zero reward-surrogate gradient in group-relative optimization.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_trajectory_curation_margin_004.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two curves against per-attempt pass rate from zero to one for eight attempts. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 1. A thin blue success-yield curve rises quickly toward one, tracing the thick purple informative-task curve below a pass rate of 0.5. The purple curve is a symmetric plateau that falls to zero at both ends, with dots at 0.34 for pass rates of 5 and 95 percent."}

*Easy fixtures yield successes most often; mid-difficulty fixtures yield contrast most often.*
:::

Choosing fixture difficulty is therefore a resource allocation decision. Hard fixtures cost about `{python} InformativeTaskFraction.attempts_low_str` attempts per harvested success, but they force the agent into unfamiliar states and expose missing recovery skills. Easy fixtures cost almost nothing per success, serving as cheap regression anchors that preserve baseline competence. For rare or high-consequence task families, low harvest yields are a worthwhile price for keeping coverage intact. Recording the sampling and retention policies alongside the corpus makes these shifts visible across retraining rounds, where evolving interfaces can invalidate older records and repeated self-selection can narrow behavioral coverage.

### Staleness and coverage narrowing {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-coverage-narrowing}

Across those retraining rounds, a trajectory recorded minutes ago is already unusable if it called a deprecated tool schema or passed a flawed grader, whereas a trace recorded months ago by an older policy remains a valid demonstration as long as the tools and environment semantics have not changed. In an evolving agent system, **staleness**\index{Staleness!trajectory corpus} therefore measures architectural incompatibility rather than chronological age. Trajectory stores prevent silent corruption by binding four provenance fields to every record: the generating policy, the environment fixture, the tool interface schema, and the grading criteria. When grading criteria change, the pipeline re-runs verification. When tool schemas change, existing records undergo schema migration and revalidation. As the policy improves, sampling shifts toward the harder edge cases the updated agent still fails.

Even when every schema and grader stays current, repeated self-training narrows behavioral coverage. Because strategies that cleared earlier filters appear more often in fine-tuning data, the updated policy reproduces those paths more often and samples them even more heavily in the next round. Left unchecked, training repeatedly on a model's own filtered outputs shrinks distributional diversity, a form of model collapse [@shumailov2024] driven by the hidden feedback loop between a model's outputs and its future training set [@sculley2015hidden]. Automated verifiers reject failures covered by their checks, but filtering alone cannot break that self-reinforcing loop; teams must measure and bound the drift directly.

Three telemetry signals warn when coverage is narrowing across rounds. Within each fixture, the number of distinct normalized action sequences falls as the policy repeats the same routines; across attempts on a fixture, pass@1 continues to rise while pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ at large $\IndependentAttemptCount$ flattens out, showing that probability mass is concentrating on familiar paths rather than discovering alternative solutions; and across the benchmark, scores on held-out task families stall even as acceptance on training fixtures climbs. Because a drop in distinct action sequences can simply mean the agent is cutting out unneeded retries, engineers read action diversity alongside held-out transfer scores: when shrinking diversity coincides with flat held-out performance, the policy is over-specializing.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$, the probability that at least one of $\IndependentAttemptCount$ sampled candidates passes, is established in @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k.
:::

Countering this narrowing requires bounding how heavily any single fixture or synthetic round can shape the dataset. At the fixture level, per-task retention caps keep easily solved problems from flooding the corpus, and deduplication filters drop identical normalized action sequences unless they occurred under genuinely different observations. Across retraining rounds, the corpus pairs synthetic runs with a permanent anchor of verified external demonstrations (such as curated human traces) that self-play cannot overwrite. Early-stopping rules halt the loop as soon as action diversity and held-out scores plateau, even if training-fixture acceptance keeps rising.

External demonstrations and held-out evaluation suites play distinct roles here. Curated human or expert demonstrations anchor the training mixture because they come from outside the current policy's habits. Protected evaluation tasks, by contrast, stay outside both training and automated selection under the development and final-test split discipline of @sec-vol3-flywheel-evaluation. Because each promotion step in a self-improvement loop consults a holdout score, the benchmark that gates round-by-round promotion acts as a development set over multiple rounds, and a separate final-test suite must verify any final generalization claim. Periodic human audits across accepted, rejected, and borderline runs catch grader shortcuts and missed edge cases before promotion, while production telemetry supplies fresh task candidates from live traffic.

### Production feedback signals {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-production-feedback}

Production sessions expose edge cases that offline fixtures never anticipated, but treating raw user actions as ground-truth labels corrupts a corpus. A user who accepts a patch without editing it may never have run the tests, and a user who abandons a session may have been interrupted. Extracting training signals from live telemetry requires treating each observed event as evidence of the user's immediate action rather than a verdict on task correctness (@tbl-vol3-trajectory-curation-feedback-signals).

| **Signal**             | **Evidence Provided**                       | **Limitation**                                                             | **Possible Learning Use**                                                           |
|:-----------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Accepted without edits | Recorded acceptance of the delivered output | The user may not have checked correctness                                  | Usability label under a declared criterion; candidate for task validation           |
| Edited or reverted     | A change to, or rejection of, the output    | May reflect correction, style, or changed requirements                     | Proposed target or comparison after checking the applicable task and context        |
| Mid-task correction    | New user guidance at a particular turn      | Does not establish the cause of the earlier behavior                       | Recovery context, intent clarification, or a candidate fixture                      |
| Retry or abandonment   | A retry or session-ending event             | Latency, cost, interruptions, and changed plans can produce the same event | Investigation or a label for the observed event, not assumed task failure           |
| Explicit rating        | The respondent's recorded assessment        | Missing responses and response selection limit population claims           | Label for a defined satisfaction criterion, not automatic proof of task correctness |

: **Production Feedback Signals**: Preserve the observed event and its context before assigning a learning role. A signal may directly label its declared criterion without establishing unrelated properties. {#tbl-vol3-trajectory-curation-feedback-signals}

Misreading these signals distorts the training set. When a user edits an agent's output to add a new requirement, the edited text answers the revised request rather than the original prompt; training on that edited output without updating the prompt teaches the model to guess unstated constraints. Likewise, pairing an agent's draft with a user's edit as a preference comparison is valid only when the context and task goal stay identical across both versions. Telemetry pipelines therefore treat missing feedback as unobserved rather than positive, check user consent and data-use permissions before ingestion, and turn recurring production failures into graded regression fixtures before feeding them into training. Together with retention caps and external anchors, these safeguards turn self-improvement into a concrete collection plan with explicit sampling budgets, automated verification stages, and human review gates. Because rollout generation scales out easily across accelerators while sandboxed verification and human review have tight throughput ceilings, the collection pipeline must pace sampling against downstream checking capacity so unverified traces never swamp staging storage.

## Collection Pipeline Architecture {#sec-vol3-flywheel-pipeline}

During a collection campaign, a fleet of rollout workers can finish hundreds of candidate traces while downstream test sandboxes are saturated. A multi-predicate check can also stall waiting on a single lagging reviewer after earlier checks have already passed. Because generation, verification, and dataset publication run at different speeds, structuring collection as an asynchronous pipeline decouples the stages within explicit capacity limits. When downstream verifiers or review queues fill up, backpressure throttles or pauses new rollouts before in-flight outputs exhaust staging storage.

### Pipeline responsibilities {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-pipeline-responsibilities}

If a rollout worker tears down its execution sandbox before persisting the candidate workspace bytes, or if a network retry submits a duplicate trace without a stable run identity, the collector either loses the evidence for an accepted run or double-counts examples in the published corpus. To give every artifact and buffer reservation an explicit owner across handoffs, the pipeline divides into four responsibilities (@tbl-vol3-pipeline-stages). These stages may share a single host or run as distributed services across a cluster; the division fixes ownership of work, state, and evidence rather than hardware layout.

| Responsibility         | Input and owned work                                                                                                    | Handoff condition                                                                                                     |
|:-----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Collection admission   | Versioned task fixture, generator configuration, permitted interactions, preassigned split group, and collection budget | Reserve capacity for admitted work and its bounded output before starting the rollout                                 |
| Rollout and capture    | Execute through the trusted harness; record the available interaction history, candidate artifact, and capture gaps     | Persist the required candidate bytes and manifest at a consistent boundary before releasing their only execution copy |
| Staging and assessment | Hold a bounded record or protected artifact references; run the selected cascade and any separately admitted review     | Record criterion-level results and the proposed learning use, including unresolved assessments                        |
| Dataset publication    | Apply the declared use, transformation, permission, and split policies to assessed records                              | Publish an identified derived version with its eligibility decision and provenance, or record another disposition     |

: **Collection responsibilities and handoffs**: Each boundary transfers identified work under a capacity and evidence contract. Completing a rollout does not guarantee task acceptance or publication as a training example. {#tbl-vol3-pipeline-stages}

At each handoff, the pipeline checks an explicit contract. In a software repair collection run, for instance, the handoff from capture to assessment binds the persisted workspace bytes (`ws_r20`) to the acceptance policy (`repair_accept_v1`) and records which execution artifacts are available for the declared learning use within the trace capture limits. The verification cascade then runs the predicates of @sec-vol3-flywheel-verification, separating whether a rollout solved the task from whether it qualifies as a demonstration, a preference pair, or a rollout fixture. If a predicate cannot be completed immediately, the pipeline records its state as `pending` or `unknown` rather than treating it as a failure. Slow stages such as human review or formal verification pull cases from a dedicated, bounded queue; transferring a record to that queue requires an acknowledgment that buffer space is reserved, so stalled reviews cannot pile up and exhaust staging storage.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Trace capture limits and retention boundaries are established in @sec-vol3-evaluation-budgets.
:::

Because distributed workers and network links fail, message delivery is retried. Every submission is therefore bound to its collection run identifier, artifact version, and assessment policy. When a retry arrives with an identical payload under the same identifier, the stage returns the existing decision. If the payload differs from the earlier submission under that identifier, the pipeline routes the conflict to an operator queue. A retry never publishes duplicate training examples or frees a staging reservation twice, which sets up the quantitative sizing of those staging reservations.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Semantic deduplication of retried writes, which acknowledges an identical retry and rejects a conflicting payload under the same identity, is established in @sec-vol3-persistence-engine-design.
:::

### Collection credits and staging reserves {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-collection-credits}

Sizing those staging reservations around average verifier throughput fails as soon as a defective test fixture or unresponsive dependency forces every verifier slot to run until its hard timeout. In steady state, when completed rollouts arrive at verification at an average rate $\ArrivalRate$ and $\WorkerCount$ equivalent verifier slots each require a mean service time $\MeanVerifierServiceTime$ per record, the pool provides an aggregate service capacity of $\WorkerCount/\MeanVerifierServiceTime$ records per second at nominal utilization $\ServingUtilization=\ArrivalRate \MeanVerifierServiceTime/\WorkerCount$. Little's law (theorem \ref{thrm-05-littles-law}) gives the mean number of records in service as $\ArrivalRate \MeanVerifierServiceTime = \ServingUtilization \WorkerCount$, so the nominal utilization is also the fraction of slots occupied on average.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Little's law, which ties mean occupancy to arrival rate and residence time, is established in @sec-vol3-kv-workload-dynamics.
:::

That steady-state baseline breaks when a stall forces every verifier execution to block until hitting its hard timeout $\VerifierTimeout$, collapsing aggregate checking capacity from $\WorkerCount/\MeanVerifierServiceTime$ to $\WorkerCount/\VerifierTimeout$. If rollouts continue arriving at rate $\ArrivalRate$, unassessed records accumulate in staging at a net rate of $\ArrivalRate - \WorkerCount/\VerifierTimeout$ records per second. If each record reserves buffer space up to a maximum per-record ceiling $\RecordSizeCeiling$, a staging storage pool of total capacity $\StagingStoreCapacity$ that is empty when the burst begins is exhausted after

$$\StagingExhaustionTime=\frac{\StagingStoreCapacity}{\left(\ArrivalRate-\WorkerCount/\VerifierTimeout\right)\RecordSizeCeiling}.$$

A store that already holds records at onset is exhausted sooner, in proportion to the space they occupy. Crossing an alert threshold does not halt staging growth immediately, because two sequential waves of records still arrive before the buffer stabilizes. First, while the controller takes $\ControllerReactionDelay$ to detect the stall and close dispatch, the dispatcher continues launching replacement rollouts, so staging keeps accumulating net reservations at rate $(\ArrivalRate-\WorkerCount/\VerifierTimeout)\RecordSizeCeiling$ throughout that delay. Second, at the moment dispatch finally closes, the rollouts still executing in the fleet hold up to $\InflightRolloutReservation$ in reservations that can all complete before stalled verifiers drain them. Subtracting both waves from total capacity $\StagingStoreCapacity$ bounds the high watermark (the fraction of the store at which the alert must trigger):

$$\text{watermark} \le 1-\frac{\InflightRolloutReservation + \ControllerReactionDelay\left(\ArrivalRate-\WorkerCount/\VerifierTimeout\right)\RecordSizeCeiling}{\StagingStoreCapacity}.$$

Notebook \ref{nbk-14-verifier-burst-exhaustion} evaluates how fast staging fills on a representative verification fleet and where dispatch must stop.

```{python}
#| label: lego-14-verifier-burst-exhaustion
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STAGING EXHAUSTION UNDER A VERIFIER TIMEOUT BURST (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-flywheel-pipeline, @nbk-14-verifier-burst-exhaustion.
# │ Goal: Show how fast reserved staging fills when service time collapses.
# │ Show: Nominal utilization, degraded capacity, exhaustion time, watermark.
# │ How: Aggregate slot capacity; reservations charged at the record ceiling.
# │ Note: Every input is hypothetical; no queueing-delay formula is applied.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Scenarios
from mlsysim.core.units import GB, MB, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_percent, fmt_qty, fmt_time

class VerifierBurstExhaustion:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical fleet, verifier pool, record ceiling, and store (scenario).
    scenario = Scenarios.VerifierTimeoutStagingBurst
    n_rollouts = scenario.rollouts
    rollout_time = scenario.rollout_time
    slots = scenario.slots
    mean_service = scenario.mean_service
    timeout = scenario.timeout
    max_record = scenario.record_ceiling
    store = scenario.store
    reaction = scenario.reaction

    # 2. EXECUTE: nominal utilization, burst growth, exhaustion, watermark.
    burst = scenario.result
    arrival = burst.arrival_rate
    capacity = burst.capacity
    rho = burst.utilization
    degraded = burst.burst_capacity
    net = burst.net_growth
    growth = burst.growth
    t_exhaust = burst.time_to_full
    inflight = burst.in_flight
    high_mark = burst.high_watermark
    high_mark_set = int(high_mark * 100) / 100

    # 3. GUARD: stable nominal case, unstable burst, watermark below its bound.
    check(0.74 < rho < 0.76, "Nominal utilization below one")
    check(net.to(1 / second).magnitude > 0, "Staging grows during the burst")
    check(0 < high_mark_set <= high_mark < 1, "Watermark within its bound")

    # 4. OUTPUT: every export is consumed in the notebook below.
    rollouts_str = fmt_int(n_rollouts)
    rollout_time_str = fmt_time(rollout_time, unit="s", precision=0)
    slots_str = fmt_int(slots)
    service_str = fmt_time(mean_service, unit="s", precision=3)
    timeout_str = fmt_time(timeout, unit="s", precision=0)
    max_record_str = fmt_memory(max_record, unit=MB, precision=0)
    store_str = fmt_memory(store, unit=GB, precision=0)
    reaction_str = fmt_time(reaction, unit="s", precision=0)
    arrival_str = fmt(arrival.to(1 / second).magnitude, precision=1)
    capacity_str = fmt(capacity.to(1 / second).magnitude, precision=1)
    rho_str = fmt(rho, precision=2)
    degraded_str = fmt(degraded.to(1 / second).magnitude, precision=1)
    net_str = fmt(net.to(1 / second).magnitude, precision=1)
    growth_str = fmt_qty(growth, "MB/s", precision=1)
    t_exhaust_str = fmt_time(t_exhaust, unit="s", precision=1)
    t_exhaust_min_str = fmt_time(t_exhaust, unit="min", precision=1)
    inflight_str = fmt_memory(inflight, unit=GB, precision=1)
    reaction_growth_str = fmt_memory(burst.reaction_growth, unit=GB, precision=1)
    high_mark_str = fmt_percent(high_mark_set, precision=0, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-14-verifier-burst-exhaustion .callout-notebook title="How long a staging store survives a timeout burst"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical collector runs `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.rollouts_str` concurrent rollouts that each take `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.rollout_time_str`. `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.slots_str` verifier slots take `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.service_str` per record on average. Each record reserves a ceiling of `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.max_record_str` in a `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.store_str` staging store. Treat completions as a steady flow and all slots as interchangeable. A defective fixture then makes every test run to its `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.timeout_str` timeout. How long until the store is fully reserved, and where must dispatch stop if the controller needs `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.reaction_str` to act?

**Math**: Rollouts complete at `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.arrival_str` records per second against a nominal capacity of `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.capacity_str`, giving a utilization of `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.rho_str`; by Little's law, that is also the average fraction of the `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.slots_str` slots in use. During the burst, capacity falls to `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.degraded_str` records per second, so staging grows by `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.net_str` records, or `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.growth_str` of reservations, every second. Starting from an empty store, it is fully reserved after `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.t_exhaust_str`, about `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.t_exhaust_min_str`. When dispatch stops, the rollouts already running still hold up to `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.inflight_str` of reservations, and growth over the `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.reaction_str` reaction delay adds `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.reaction_growth_str`. Subtracting both from the `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.store_str` store places the high watermark at or below `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.high_mark_str` of the store.

**Systems insight**: Size staging buffers for service-time collapses rather than nominal steady-state utilization. Even at a modest nominal utilization of `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.rho_str`, a verifier stall fills available storage in only `{python} VerifierBurstExhaustion.t_exhaust_min_str`. The exhaustion time $\StagingExhaustionTime$ shrinks proportionally as the record ceiling $\RecordSizeCeiling$ increases and scales linearly with total store size $\StagingStoreCapacity$. Watermarks must account for work already in flight and controller reaction latency, backed by hard credit caps when feedback loops lag.

:::

The in-flight term in that headroom shows why admission control must count unfinished work rather than queue depth. Queue length reflects past arrivals, while rollouts admitted before a verifier stall complete and emit records long after the dispatcher stops issuing new work. Admission controllers therefore limit both the count of active records and their aggregate reserved bytes, and they charge each reservation at the per-record ceiling $\RecordSizeCeiling$ rather than the mean size, because mean sizes set steady-state storage while the ceiling bounds a worst-case burst.

A **collection credit**\index{Collection credit!definition}[^fn-credit-flow-curation] enforces both constraints through a single accounting token: every admitted rollout acquires one credit from a shared pool, reserving storage for its maximum possible payload throughout rollout execution, intermediate staging, and downstream assessment. The credit returns to the pool only when the record reaches a durable terminal disposition or completes an acknowledged handoff to another capacity-controlled queue. Consequently, every unit of pending work is explicitly accounted for across the entire cluster. When a trajectory exceeds its expected allocation, the capture harness enforces an explicit truncation policy rather than silently clipping required state. For example, it records the partial execution trace with marked omissions and flags the artifact as ineligible for training regimes that require full fidelity. Because one credit spans all four responsibilities, the pool also bounds work that has left the collector but not yet reached a disposition (@fig-vol3-collection-pipeline).

[^fn-credit-flow-curation]: **Credit-Based Flow Control**: The mechanism originates in network switches, where a transmitter may forward a cell only while holding a credit for a free downstream buffer slot, so buffers cannot overflow however bursty the traffic [@kung1994credit]. The receiver returns the credit only after draining the slot, the analog of returning a collection credit upon durable disposition. \index{Credit-based flow control!collection credits}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Credit windows between cooperating agents, and the throughput a window of fixed size allows, are developed in @sec-vol3-multiagent-credit-flow-control.
:::

::: {#fig-vol3-collection-pipeline data-explore="original-v3-collection-pipeline" data-explore-key="vol3:fig-vol3-collection-pipeline" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Collection Credits Across Four Responsibilities**: Each admitted run holds one credit through rollout, capture, staging, and assessment. The credit returns to the pool only when the record reaches a durable disposition or an acknowledged transfer to another bounded owner, such as the review queue. A watermark derived from in-flight work slows dispatch before the pool is exhausted, and a hard limit stops admission when that feedback arrives late." fig-alt="A vertical credit pool gauge on the left holds ten credit slots, six filled from the bottom and labeled in flight. A red line at the top of the gauge is labeled hard limit, stops admission, and a dashed line two slots below it is labeled watermark, slows dispatch. An arrow labeled acquire leads from the pool to a single bar divided into rollout, capture, staging, and assessment, with a violet bracket beneath it spanning all four segments and a single credit swatch labeled one credit held per run. From the bar, arrows lead to three boxes: dataset publication, derived version; diagnostic pool, or comparison; and review queue, unresolved hold. Dashed violet lines from all three join a return path along the bottom of the figure into the base of the pool, labeled credit returned on durable disposition or acknowledged transfer."}
![](images/svg/vol3-collection-pipeline.svg)
:::

The credit pool directly bounds the count and aggregate record volume of all outstanding runs. This mechanism governs staging buffers, not auxiliary execution resources. Accelerator memory for model inference, sandbox container filesystems, verifier scratch disks, and external object stores each require separate capacity pools with independent accounting. Storing a lightweight URI reference in a message queue does not bound the multi-gigabyte container image or execution trace to which it points. Robust admission controllers verify reservations across all requisite resource pools up front. This pre-allocation invariant ensures that a pipeline stage never acquires one scarce resource, such as an accelerator slot, only to block indefinitely waiting for an unreserved downstream buffer. That credit bound holds even when a completion burst arrives while verification is paused, as notebook \ref{nbk-14-sizing-intermediate-staging-buffers-and} works out for a hypothetical collector.

```{python}
#| label: lego-14-sizing-intermediate-staging-buffers-and
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BOUNDED COLLECTION CREDITS
# │ Goal: Account for in-flight outputs before a completion burst arrives.
# │ Scope: Hypothetical fixed-size ceiling and deterministic verifier service.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim.core.units import MB, MiB, byte, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_qty, fmt_memory

class CollectionCreditCapacity:
    """Reserved captured-record capacity; not total pipeline memory or throughput."""

    # 1. LOAD — stipulated inputs, not hardware measurements.
    credits = 12
    queued = 4
    running = 8
    max_record = 2 * MiB
    verifiers = 2
    service_time = 10 * second

    # 2. CALCULATE — no new admissions during this drain experiment.
    outstanding = queued + running
    unused_credits = credits - outstanding
    queued_capacity = queued * max_record
    running_reservation = running * max_record
    record_capacity = credits * max_record
    drain_waves = math.ceil(outstanding / verifiers)
    drain_time = drain_waves * service_time

    # 3. ASSERT — counts and binary byte quantities retain their boundaries.
    check(outstanding == 12, "outstanding")
    check(unused_credits == 0, "unused_credits")
    check(queued_capacity.to(MiB).magnitude == 8, "queued_capacity")
    check(running_reservation.to(MiB).magnitude == 16, "running_reservation")
    check(record_capacity.to(MiB).magnitude == 24, "record_capacity")
    check(queued_capacity + running_reservation == record_capacity, "reserved_sum")
    check(drain_waves == 6, "drain_waves")
    check(drain_time.to(second).magnitude == 60, "drain_time")

    # 4. OUTPUT — every formatted value is consumed below.
    credits_str = fmt_int(credits)
    queued_count_str = fmt_int(queued)
    running_count_str = fmt_int(running)
    max_record_str = fmt_memory(max_record, unit=MB, precision=2)
    verifiers_str = fmt_int(verifiers)
    service_str = fmt_qty(service_time, second, precision=0)
    outstanding_str = fmt_int(outstanding)
    unused_str = fmt_int(unused_credits)
    queued_str = fmt_memory(queued_capacity, unit=MB, precision=2)
    running_str = fmt_memory(running_reservation, unit=MB, precision=2)
    capacity_str = fmt_memory(record_capacity, unit=MB, precision=2)
    capacity_bytes_str = fmt_memory(record_capacity, unit=byte, precision=0)
    waves_str = fmt_int(drain_waves)
    drain_str = fmt_qty(drain_time, second, precision=0)
```

::: {#nbk-14-sizing-intermediate-staging-buffers-and .callout-notebook title="Reserve capacity before the completion burst"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical collector provisions `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.credits_str` end-to-end credits, each reserving a per-record ceiling of about `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.max_record_str`. Currently, `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.queued_count_str` records sit staged in storage and `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.running_count_str` rollouts are actively executing, each holding an allocated credit while verification is temporarily paused. May the dispatcher admit an additional rollout? Furthermore, once all active rollouts finish and verification resumes, how long will this accumulated cohort take to drain?

**Variables**: `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.verifiers_str` verifiers each assess one record at a time in exactly `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.service_str`, including durable disposition; no new rollout is admitted during the drain, and transfer and publication add no delay.

**Math**: The `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.outstanding_str` outstanding runs hold every credit: staged records reserve `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.queued_str` and running rollouts `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.running_str`, for `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.capacity_str` (exactly `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.capacity_bytes_str`) with `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.unused_str` credits free, so the dispatcher admits nothing. Draining the queue takes ⌈`{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.outstanding_str` / `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.verifiers_str`⌉ = `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.waves_str` waves of `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.service_str`, or `{python} CollectionCreditCapacity.drain_str`.

**Systems insight**: Total byte consumption is strictly bounded by credits multiplied by the ceiling ($\RecordSizeCeiling$), independent of arrival timing, while drain latency scales as ⌈credits / verifiers⌉ times service time. Adding verifiers accelerates queue drainage without increasing the byte bound; expanding credits raises both. Engineers should dimension credit pools against physical staging limits and scale verifiers to meet drain deadlines, treating a slower assessment as a longer drain with the reservation still actively held.

:::

The two models bound different quantities. Arrival and service rates govern how rapidly an outage consumes available headroom, while credit limits cap total buffer consumption regardless of timing. Production telemetry must continuously track queue depths, allocated vs. physically consumed bytes, the age of the oldest pending assessment, verification pass rates, and downstream sink throughput. Retries, escalated evaluations, and diagnostic reviews must all consume allocations from this same credit pool. When external dependencies fail, failure containment mechanisms prevent repeated re-verification attempts from amplifying an isolated service outage into cluster-wide failure, leaving steady-state capacity planning to determine which stage limits throughput when the pipeline is healthy.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Circuit breakers, coordinated retries, and bulkheads that keep retry amplification from spreading a dependency outage are established in @sec-vol3-sagas-containment.
:::

### The collection bottleneck {#sec-vol3-flywheel-bottleneck}

Under-provisioning cheap CPU verifier slots can throttle an entire accelerator fleet, leaving expensive generation hardware sitting idle while trajectories wait to be checked. While credit controls prevent staging buffers from overflowing during an outage, steady-state capacity planning compares generation, verification, and storage to find where throughput actually binds. With $\AcceleratorCount$ accelerators each spending $\AttemptGenerationTime$ accelerator-seconds per attempt, generation has a service ceiling of $\AcceleratorCount / \AttemptGenerationTime$ attempts per second. With $\WorkerCount$ verifier slots and expected slot service time $\ExpectedCheckingTime$ per attempt from @eq-verifier-cost-cascade, assessment has a service ceiling of $\WorkerCount / \ExpectedCheckingTime$. Charging every write at its per-record ceiling $\RecordSizeCeiling$ gives a conservative provisioned storage rate of $\DurableStoreWriteBandwidth / \RecordSizeCeiling$ for sustained write bandwidth $\DurableStoreWriteBandwidth$. With enough credits, work, and scheduling capacity to saturate the stages, the idealized planning rate $\SustainableAttemptRate$ is:

$$\SustainableAttemptRate=\min\left(\frac{\AcceleratorCount}{\AttemptGenerationTime},\ \frac{\WorkerCount}{\ExpectedCheckingTime},\ \frac{\DurableStoreWriteBandwidth}{\RecordSizeCeiling}\right).$$ {#eq-vol3-trajectory-curation-throughput-bound}

@Eq-vol3-trajectory-curation-throughput-bound identifies the binding stage in this stipulated model. Its planned admitted-record rate is $\SustainableAttemptRate \cdot \AdmissionRouteYield$, where $\AdmissionRouteYield$ is the route yield. Actual throughput can be lower because of credits, scheduling, or another shared service. Smaller writes can exceed the conservative storage term, so that term alone does not diagnose an observed storage bottleneck.

The bound separates the stage that limits throughput from the stage that drives cost. In the illustrated low-priced deterministic route, verifiers occupy CPU slots that cost pennies per hour compared with accelerator instances, yet starving that pool stalls the whole collector. Under the notebook's active-resource accounting, unused capacity is redeployed or unbilled, and generation compute and task yield dominate the charge per admitted record. A dedicated fleet billed during idle wall time has a different cost boundary. Deterministic verification is not inexpensive for every workload. A model judge or a human reviewer can change that split, and Exercise 5 in @sec-vol3-14_trajectory_curation-exercises prices a route in which human review dominates. Notebook \ref{nbk-14-collection-bottleneck} evaluates this economic trade-off on a representative deployment.

```{python}
#| label: lego-14-collection-bottleneck
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COLLECTION BOTTLENECK AND COST PER ADMITTED RECORD (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-trajectory-curation-throughput-bound,
# │          @nbk-14-collection-bottleneck.
# │ Goal: Find the binding stage and split cost between generation and checking.
# │ Show: Three planning rates, slots needed, active charge per record and split.
# │ How: Reuses the cascade notebook's expected slot time and yield; registry
# │      inference GPU-hour rate; other inputs hypothetical.
# │ Note: Ceiling-charged writes; active-time billing; slot price stipulated.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import MB, hour, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_percent, fmt_qty, fmt_time, fmt_usd

class CollectionBottleneck:
    # 1. LOAD: cascade results, registry accelerator rate, hypothetical fleet.
    slot_time = VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.expected_s[0] * second
    route_yield = VerificationCascadeEconomicsThroughput.yield_rate
    accel_rate = Infrastructure.Pricing.Cloud.GpuInferencePerHour.rate
    slot_rate = 0.04 * USD / hour  # hypothetical verifier-slot price
    n_accel = 64
    gen_time = 60 * second  # accelerator-seconds per attempt
    slots = 4
    write_bw = 200 * (MB / second)
    max_record = 8 * MB

    # 2. EXECUTE: planning rates, binding stage, slots to unbind, active cost split.
    gen_ceiling = (n_accel / gen_time).to(1 / second)
    verify_ceiling = (slots / slot_time).to(1 / second)
    store_ceiling = (write_bw / max_record).to(1 / second)
    theta = min(gen_ceiling, verify_ceiling, store_ceiling)
    slots_needed = math.ceil((gen_ceiling * slot_time).to("").magnitude)
    gen_cost = (gen_time * accel_rate).to(USD)
    verify_cost = (slot_time * slot_rate).to(USD)
    per_admitted = (gen_cost + verify_cost) / route_yield
    verify_share = (verify_cost / (gen_cost + verify_cost)).to("").magnitude

    # 3. GUARD: verification binds at the stated slot count; enough slots unbind it.
    check(verify_ceiling < gen_ceiling < store_ceiling, "Verification binds first")
    check(theta == verify_ceiling, "Planning rate equals the verification ceiling")
    check(slots_needed * 1 / slot_time >= gen_ceiling, "Enough slots to match generation")
    check(verify_share < 0.01, "Checking is a small share of cost")

    # 4. OUTPUT: every export is consumed in the notebook below.
    n_accel_str = fmt_int(n_accel)
    gen_time_str = fmt_time(gen_time, unit="s", precision=0)
    slots_str = fmt_int(slots)
    slot_time_str = fmt_time(slot_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    write_bw_str = fmt_qty(write_bw, "MB/s", precision=0)
    max_record_str = fmt_memory(max_record, unit=MB, precision=0)
    accel_rate_str = fmt_usd(accel_rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude, precision=2)
    slot_rate_str = fmt_usd(slot_rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude, precision=2)
    yield_str = fmt_percent(route_yield, precision=2, style="prose")
    gen_ceiling_str = fmt(gen_ceiling.to(1 / second).magnitude, precision=2)
    verify_ceiling_str = fmt(verify_ceiling.to(1 / second).magnitude, precision=2)
    store_ceiling_str = fmt(store_ceiling.to(1 / second).magnitude, precision=0)
    slots_needed_str = fmt_int(slots_needed)
    per_admitted_str = fmt_usd(per_admitted.to(USD).magnitude, precision=2)
    verify_share_str = fmt_percent(verify_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    gen_cost_str = fmt_usd(gen_cost.to(USD).magnitude, precision=3)
    per_admitted_half_str = fmt_usd(2 * per_admitted.to(USD).magnitude, precision=2)
    half_yield_str = fmt_percent(route_yield / 2, precision=2, style="prose")
    idle_str = fmt_percent(1 - (verify_ceiling / gen_ceiling).to("").magnitude, precision=1, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-14-collection-bottleneck .callout-notebook title="The cheapest stage can set the rate"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical collector uses `{python} CollectionBottleneck.n_accel_str` accelerators, each spending `{python} CollectionBottleneck.gen_time_str` of accelerator time per attempt at `{python} CollectionBottleneck.accel_rate_str` per hour. It checks attempts with the admission route of notebook \ref{nbk-14-verification-cascade-economics-and-throughput}, whose cheaper order occupies `{python} CollectionBottleneck.slot_time_str` of slot time per attempt and admits `{python} CollectionBottleneck.yield_str` of attempts, on `{python} CollectionBottleneck.slots_str` verifier slots priced at `{python} CollectionBottleneck.slot_rate_str` per slot-hour. Records of at most `{python} CollectionBottleneck.max_record_str` go to a store that sustains `{python} CollectionBottleneck.write_bw_str`. Assume sufficient end-to-end credits and no further shared service bottleneck, charge each write at its record ceiling, and bill only active accelerator and occupied verifier time, with unused capacity redeployed or unbilled. Which stage binds this planning model, and what is the active-resource charge per admitted record?

**Math**: By @eq-vol3-trajectory-curation-throughput-bound, generation supports `{python} CollectionBottleneck.n_accel_str` / `{python} CollectionBottleneck.gen_time_str` = `{python} CollectionBottleneck.gen_ceiling_str` attempts per second, assessment `{python} CollectionBottleneck.slots_str` / `{python} CollectionBottleneck.slot_time_str` = `{python} CollectionBottleneck.verify_ceiling_str`, and conservative provisioned storage supports `{python} CollectionBottleneck.write_bw_str` / `{python} CollectionBottleneck.max_record_str` = `{python} CollectionBottleneck.store_ceiling_str`. Assessment binds in this model, and matching generation needs `{python} CollectionBottleneck.gen_ceiling_str` × `{python} CollectionBottleneck.slot_time_str`, rounded up to `{python} CollectionBottleneck.slots_needed_str` slots. Generation costs `{python} CollectionBottleneck.gen_cost_str` per attempt; adding checking and dividing by the yield gives `{python} CollectionBottleneck.per_admitted_str` per admitted record, of which checking is `{python} CollectionBottleneck.verify_share_str`.

**Systems insight**: Throughput bottlenecks and cost drivers are often decoupled. In this scenario, running only `{python} CollectionBottleneck.slots_str` inexpensive verifier slots leaves `{python} CollectionBottleneck.idle_str` of generation capacity unused. Despite this bottleneck, the financial cost of an admitted record is dominated by generation expense divided by yield, following the cost per accepted task formulation (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task). Adding verifier slots raises the idealized rate until generation saturates while leaving the active-resource charge per record unchanged. With a dedicated fleet billed during idle wall time, greater utilization can instead lower the bill per emitted record. Holding active work per attempt and resource rates fixed, halving the yield to `{python} CollectionBottleneck.half_yield_str` doubles the unrounded cost per admitted record, displayed to the nearest cent as `{python} CollectionBottleneck.per_admitted_half_str`. Fixture design and sampling policy control that yield; their measured cost and coverage consequences determine whether a change is worthwhile.

:::

### Artifact capture and resource release {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-artifact-capture}

Tearing down a rollout container before its logs and workspace diffs reach durable storage destroys the only copy of the attempt, while reassigning a pooled container before background writers exit lets a stale rollout pollute the next task. Collection pipelines therefore inherit the runtime's sandbox lifecycle and reset contracts. Rollout workers must persist all candidate artifacts, interaction traces, and evaluation evidence to durable storage before tearing down the execution sandbox. A pooled environment cannot be reassigned until background writer processes terminate, stale network credentials and access tokens are revoked, and filesystem reset postconditions pass. If a downstream verification stage needs interactive access to unpersisted sandbox state, it must hold that environment under an explicit time-bounded lease and operational budget; otherwise, the checker logs the assessment as unavailable and releases the host.

When a worker's dispatch lease expires, expiration does not instantly terminate the executing process or roll back its external side effects. A replacement worker must therefore establish explicit ownership and verify fresh admission checks, while late-arriving outputs from the orphaned worker remain strictly quarantined to their original run. Similarly, if container cleanup fails or an external side effect leaves an indeterminate state, the owning process retains responsibility under the trajectory saga, even if the associated trajectory is discarded from training. Releasing a collection credit frees buffer staging, but it does not absolve the runtime of its teardown and cleanup obligations. Once physical movement from execution to durable disposition is bounded and accounted for, data governance determines artifact admissibility. It asks which upstream source versions justify inclusion, what lossy or privacy-preserving transformations were applied, and which dataset split partitions and license restrictions govern the resulting weights.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The trajectory saga, which keeps a compensation obligation open while an external effect remains unresolved, is established in @sec-vol3-sagas-architecture.
:::

## Trajectory Provenance Tracking {#sec-vol3-flywheel-provenance}

When an automated scrubbing pass strips sensitive network addresses from raw collection record `trace_r19_01` (from collection run `collection_run_r19_01` and candidate workspace `ws_r20`) to create `trace_r19_01_redacted_v1`, the transformed artifact cannot silently overwrite the source record and inherit its admission labels. Months after an execution trace enters a training corpus, curators must still be able to answer which collection run produced the sequence, which validation criteria were checked against which environment fixtures, whether the organization retains legal permission to train on the incorporated source code or API payloads, and whether sanitization invalidated the runtime state that justified the agent's next action. A preserved execution trace and its evaluation scores cannot answer these questions on their own. In a production curation pipeline, **provenance**\index{Provenance!trajectory record} provides the immutable, versioned record that answers them across every derivation of a trace, giving `trace_r19_01_redacted_v1` an independent identity and its own admission decision.

### The lineage envelope {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-lineage-envelope}

When a source repository revokes training permission or a grader bug invalidates a week of checks, an unindexed store of raw JSON traces cannot identify which corpus members must be pulled. A **lineage envelope**\index{Lineage envelope!definition}[^fn-provenance-why-where] prevents that blind spot by recording the origin, dependencies, transformations, and admission decisions of each individual record version. @Tbl-vol3-provenance-schema outlines its six dimensions. Rather than embedding inline copies of sensitive or high-volume execution state, envelope fields point to content-addressed, access-controlled artifacts.

[^fn-provenance-why-where]: **Why- and Where-Provenance**: Database research distinguished two questions about a derived datum: which source records justify its existence (why-provenance) and which source locations its values were copied from (where-provenance) [@buneman2001why]. A trajectory record needs both. Where-provenance traces each retained field to the run, event, and transformation that produced it, and why-provenance traces its admission to the assessments that justified it, so a withdrawn source or a revised criterion can be followed to every affected corpus member. \index{Provenance!why and where}

| Record dimension         | Information to bind                                                                                                                          | Question it answers                                                  |
|:-------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Collection identity      | Run, task, fixture, candidate, and source-record versions; sampling or selection policy                                                      | Which attempt and inputs does this record represent?                 |
| Generation configuration | Available model and adapter identity, tokenizer, delivered-context references, tool interfaces, harness configuration, and sampling settings | What generated and mediated the represented proposals?               |
| Environment and capture  | Relevant initial-state and dependency versions, operation/result references, retained boundaries, omissions, and unresolved effects          | Which interactions and evidence are available, and what is missing?  |
| Assessment               | Criterion and grader versions, per-criterion verdicts, evidence references, assessment time, and intended learning use                       | What was checked, on which artifact, for which admission decision?   |
| Transformation           | Parent-record identity, transformation implementation/configuration, changed fields, derived identity, and revalidation results              | How does the emitted view differ from the source?                    |
| Use and partition        | Permission decision and scope, retention restrictions, split/group assignment, and corpus membership                                         | Where may this version go, and which evaluation boundary follows it? |

: **Trajectory lineage envelope**: Versioned references connect a record to its origin and subsequent decisions. Their presence does not certify correctness, complete capture, or permission for every use. {#tbl-vol3-provenance-schema}

The envelope must record only what the runtime interfaces actually reveal. When an agent executes against locally controlled model weights, the envelope binds the loaded base model and adapter checkpoint digests. Hosted inference endpoints, however, typically expose only a reported version string and request configuration; in those cases, the envelope documents those exact parameters rather than fabricating an unverifiable weight hash. Similarly, a prompt-template identifier fails to capture dynamic context injected at runtime, and a container base-image digest omits mutable mounted volumes or external network state. Systems engineers must document omissions explicitly rather than relying on identifiers of ambiguous scope.

Evaluation assessments bind directly to the exact byte representation tested. If a trajectory earns a passing score on a targeted capability test, that verdict applies only to that evaluated representation; any pending criterion remains pending when the record enters cold storage. The downstream evaluation cascade alone determines whether the available evidence authorizes a specific learning use, and cryptographic integrity checks then verify that the assessed byte representation is the exact one a downstream trainer reads.

### Integrity and authentication {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-integrity-authentication}

A trainer decides what to train on by reading the corpus manifest, so it must be able to confirm two things before the first gradient. The first is that the manifest is the one curation issued. The second is that no record was altered or swapped after admission, whether by a broken pipeline script or by anyone with write access to the store. Integrity mechanisms answer those two questions. They establish unmodified bytes, not correct content or permitted use. A cryptographic digest identifies a specified byte representation under standard collision-resistance assumptions. For that digest to remain meaningful across system components, the lineage envelope must fix both the canonical serialization scheme and the schema version over which the hash was calculated. Comparing an artifact against an expected digest detects bit corruption and unauthorized edits. Storing an unauthenticated digest directly beside mutable content in an object store, however, provides no protection, because an adversary or a broken pipeline script can overwrite the data and the digest together.

To guarantee authenticity, an authenticated manifest cryptographically binds expected artifact digests and associated metadata to a trusted issuing authority. Systems commonly use a message authentication code (MAC), such as HMAC as specified in RFC 2104 [@krawczyk1997hmac], computed with a secret key held outside the dataset in a key management service. Because any party holding a shared symmetric key can forge a valid MAC, production architectures often prefer asymmetric digital signatures (such as Ed25519) when datasets are distributed across multiple worker nodes. The manifest must record the cryptographic algorithm, key version, and authorized issuing scope, and key rotation policies must match the operational lifetime of the corpus. Verification confirms only that the authenticated byte representation has not changed since issuance; it covers nothing outside that boundary.

Cryptographic integrity must not be confused with semantic correctness. A faithfully authenticated trajectory trace can still hold hallucinated model outputs, an erroneous grader verdict, or private data that downstream consumers are prohibited from seeing. Similarly, computing a Merkle root[^fn-merkle-tree-curation] over captured execution events proves that a given event belongs to the recorded tree, but it proves nothing about execution events that the logging harness dropped or failed to observe. Claims about trajectory reproducibility must therefore stay within the reconstruction and re-execution boundaries established in @sec-vol3-persistence-replay.

[^fn-merkle-tree-curation]: **Merkle Tree**: A tree in which each internal node holds the hash of its children, introduced to build digital signatures from a conventional one-way function [@merkle1988digital]. Its useful property is that proving one leaf belongs under a trusted root needs only the sibling hashes along one path, logarithmic in the number of leaves. A corpus manifest can therefore commit to millions of record digests under one root and still verify a single member cheaply, but the root commits only to the leaves that were hashed. \index{Merkle tree!corpus manifest}

### Derived records {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-derived-records}

Because an authenticated source record is immutable, scrubbing a private file path or API token from a recorded trace in place would break its digest and erase the only copy of what actually ran, often severing the causal link that justified the agent's next command. At the same time, the data minimization and disclosure boundaries established in @sec-vol3-evaluation-budgets-disclosure must be enforced before trajectory content enters an ingestion queue, a model-assisted curation worker, or a training store. To resolve that tension, a **derived record**\index{Derived record!definition} is always created as a new version rather than an in-place modification. The derived record binds a reference to its parent trace, the versioned redaction policy and implementation, the explicit set of altered or excised fields, and any intentionally withheld content. Lineage references do not grant read authorization to restricted raw data, and systems must store original raw bytes only where retention policies explicitly permit them. When source records reach their retention expiration limit and are purged, the lineage envelope documents that boundary directly; retaining a cryptographic hash is not the same as retaining the source data. The source also keeps a reverse reference to each derived version, so that a later correction or withdrawal at the source reaches every artifact derived from it (@fig-vol3-provenance-envelope).

::: {#fig-vol3-provenance-envelope fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**A Derived Record and Its Lineage**: Redaction produces a new record version instead of editing the source. The derived record carries its parent reference, the fields its transformation changed or omitted, and the source's split group, but its assessment is pending until revalidation decides what the new view still supports. The source keeps a reverse reference, so a later correction or withdrawal can reach every derived version." fig-alt="A source record card labeled trace_r19_01 lists collection identity, generation configuration, environment and capture, assessment, use and partition, and reverse references. An arrow from the source passes through a redaction box, versioned policy, to a derived record card labeled trace_r19_01_redacted_v1 listing parent reference, changed fields and omissions, same split group, and a dotted row reading assessment: pending. A solid violet arrow labeled parent runs from the parent reference row back to the source's collection identity row, and a dashed violet arrow labeled correction, withdrawal runs from the source's reverse references row to the bottom of the derived card. From the pending assessment row an arrow leads to a revalidate box reading what the view supports, then down to an admission box reading declared use, or withheld."}
![](images/svg/vol3-provenance-envelope.svg)
:::

Heuristic pattern matching and named-entity recognition models act as screening mechanisms rather than complete sanitization guarantees. Engineers must validate these detectors across the full output pipeline using realistic end-to-end test cases, including deeply nested payloads and generated metadata. Synthetic canaries provide an empirical measure of detector recall. The curation audit log must record how many canaries were injected, how many escaped detection, which semantic classes and text transformations were tested, and where the inspection boundary was applied. Observing zero canary escapes bounds the leak probability only for the evaluated canary distribution. False positives carry their own cost, because over-aggressive scrubbing strips necessary context and distorts the training signal.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Canary values, planted synthetic secrets whose escape reveals a leaking path, are established in @sec-vol3-security-detectors-canaries.
:::

When scrubbing identifiers across multi-step interactions, curators use consistent pseudonyms to preserve relational dependencies across turns while preventing identity linkage beyond the access scope that the trace's disclosure boundary permits. Tokenization effects require careful handling: replacing an identifier with a fixed-width placeholder often alters the sequence's token count and attention boundaries because a placeholder string rarely splits into the same number of subword tokens as the original identifier, shifting every subsequent token index and misaligning any token-level loss masks that were indexed against the unredacted transcript. Similarly, reserializing a structured payload can preserve outer JSON or YAML formatting while silently breaking nested shell escaping, regular expression matches, or tool invocation syntax. Consequently, checking that an artifact parses successfully is distinct from verifying that it still supports the intended learning target.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Re-verifying selected response spans against token offsets after templating or redaction shifts token boundaries is developed in @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-template-rendering.
:::

Revalidation must systematically test every property that the transformation could have influenced. This includes validating record structure, ensuring action-observation consistency, verifying that the sanitized context still justifies the target action, and re-evaluating any criteria whose supporting evidence was altered. If a transformation modifies executable code or environment-dependent identifiers, the pipeline must execute the code against an isolated, authorized test fixture to obtain fresh runtime evidence, while archiving prior execution logs as historical artifacts.

::: {#exmp-14-derived-record-admission .callout-example title="A transformed record needs a new decision"}

**Scenario**: During a collection run, an agent's observation records a private system path that a subsequent diagnostic command references, and the source trace captures the successful output of that command. The curation pipeline replaces the path with a sanitized placeholder throughout `trace_r19_01_redacted_v1`.

**Diagnosis**: The recorded execution output remains valid evidence only for the original run bound to `trace_r19_01`; the agent never executed the sanitized placeholder path. The curator must determine whether the sanitized observation and the subsequent command still constitute a coherent learning example. A consistent placeholder can teach an agent how to parse and inspect arbitrary paths without exposing production directory structures. However, replaying the trajectory against an active execution harness requires an authorized, compatible mock fixture; otherwise, the substituted path fails to resolve. If the substitution obscures the causal distinction that prompted the agent's action, the pipeline must reject the target for supervised training or withhold the record. The derived record inherits the source's task grouping and train/test split assignment, while all pending evaluation verdicts remain pending until formal revalidation completes.

**Systems lesson**: Cryptographic integrity establishes which source artifact was transformed, whereas revalidation establishes what the transformed trajectory teaches. Neither operation can alter what physically occurred during the original execution run.

:::

### Use permission and withdrawal {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-permission-withdrawal}

Permission to execute an agent against a task fixture or inspect an internal repository does not convey permission to retain its artifacts, fine-tune models on its data, or publish the resulting corpus. The lineage envelope must record the explicit licensing constraints, the evidentiary basis for data retention, and the designated policy authority or human reviewer who approved data usage. This accounting must cover both the primary task assets and all third-party software dependencies pulled into the environment during execution. Automated license detectors and embedding-based similarity screens help identify suspect components, but they serve as screening tools rather than autonomous legal adjudicators.

When provenance evidence is ambiguous or incomplete, the curation pipeline must withhold the record from downstream consumers while logging the specific withholding rationale. This quarantine is use-specific: an asset held from public pretraining might remain eligible for internal safety evaluations. Furthermore, use-permission holds operate independently of task failure labels, confidentiality tiers, and fault-containment quarantine. Resolving a safety fault or task defect does not automatically grant data-usage clearance.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
⇄ **Contrast:** Incident containment, which holds the work a suspect trajectory might touch rather than withholding a record from one use, is established in @sec-vol3-sagas-quarantine.
:::

Approved data permissions operate under strict temporal and organizational scopes. To enforce policy changes, reverse references must connect each source record to its derived views, tokenized dataset partitions, and published corpus manifests. When an upstream data provider revokes permission, or when an organization updates its privacy policies, the system must propagate the restriction or withdrawal to every downstream artifact. The ingestion pipeline immediately halts new admissions under the revoked policy, while the catalog traces all distributed artifacts. Deleting a record from an active storage bucket leaves distributed offline copies and completed model parameter updates intact; managing those downstream exposures requires explicit operational ownership, retraining schedules, and audited unlearning procedures.

::: {#chk-14-recovery-curation-hygiene .callout-checkpoint title="Defend a derived record's use"}

Each bullet asks for a decision a curator makes before a derived record ships.

- [ ] **Integrity vs. truth**: A manifest's MAC verifies. Decide which of these it establishes: the bytes are unmodified, the grader verdict is correct, the record is permitted for training.
- [ ] **Transformation**: A replacement preserves JSON parsing but changes a path used by a later action. Which historical evidence remains valid, and which learning-use checks must be repeated before admission?
- [ ] **Screening**: A detector test inserts canaries of three classes and observes zero escapes. What claim can the report make, and which record classes remain untested?
- [ ] **Lineage**: A redacted record's source task is in the final-test group. Decide whether the redacted version may enter training, and name what must happen when an admitted source is later withdrawn.

:::

A well-architected trajectory record has a verifiable origin, an explicit transformation history, a legally scoped permission envelope, and preserved evaluation boundaries. Connecting an execution trace through this provenance graph into a corpus manifest gives membership a precise meaning: verified fitness for a declared learning consumer. Carrying one record through every stage shows how these decisions fit together.

## Case Study: Curating the Repair Record {#sec-vol3-flywheel-synthesis}

The recovery run `collection_run_r19_01`, whose targets @sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-conditioning-evidence selected, exercises each stage of that admission and provenance chain. Its refused edit, schema inspection, and corrected edit produced `ws_r20`, which satisfied `repair_accept_v1`. The raw trace `trace_r19_01` records that sequence without altering any earlier record, neither the pending trial verdict on `ws_r19` nor the unresolved earlier test operation `test_r18`. The curation question is which parts of this record may enter a learning artifact, for which consumer, and on what evidence.

The training objective is recovery from harness refusals, the residual behavior that the campaign's probes left with the model. The target policy `recovery_targets_v1` already fixed which tokens contribute direct supervised loss: the schema query `e3`, the corrected edit `e4`, and the final summary `e6`. The refused proposal `e2`, the test summary `e5`, the task prompt, and the intermediate tool responses stay as conditioning context. Target selection is only the first stage of admission. The record that actually enters a corpus is a transformed view of `trace_r19_01`, so the remaining stages must verify that view, bind its provenance, and publish it to a manifest.

### Admission of the derived view {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-derived-view-admission}

Replacing sensitive fixture paths in `trace_r19_01` with synthetic placeholders produces `trace_r19_01_redacted_v1`, but if that redaction strips the file names the agent needed to deduce the schema, training on the redacted trace teaches the model to guess rather than inspect. While the underlying execution stems directly from the original run, admission filtering must verify whether this sanitized view preserves the causal chain of the recovery lesson rather than assuming the raw run's pass carries over. The admission pipeline does not demand byte-for-byte fidelity with historical environment state; it requires that the transformed trace still support supervised imitation of the selected targets. @Tbl-vol3-synthesis-trajectory-roles evaluates this derived view against the curation cascade's admission predicates, where each passing verdict in a production manifest links directly to an underlying verification log.

| Admission predicate                                   | Evidence and decision for this record                                                                                                                           | Remaining boundary                                                                                                                                                                  |
|:------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Record adequacy, $\text{chk}_{\text{record}}$         | The retained source and transformation records preserve the relevant delivered context, event associations, refusal, correction, and candidate-specific results | Retaining the malformed proposal provides necessary conditioning context without selecting it as a supervised training target                                                       |
| Permitted use, $\text{chk}_{\text{use}}$              | The approved-use decision covers this derived view and imitation use; its source task group was assigned to training before collection                          | Path redaction maintains the original task group and split assignment without granting broader permissions or creating an independent evaluation task                               |
| Process conditions, $\text{chk}_{\text{proc,demo}}$   | The declared assessment permits correction of this malformed proposal and supports the required authority, resource, and residual-duty conditions               | Because the harness rejected the malformed proposal prior to dispatch, no unauthorized disk modifications occurred; other prohibited operations require distinct safety evaluations |
| Outcome criteria, $\text{chk}_{\text{out,demo}}$      | The collection's source assessment satisfies `repair_accept_v1` for `ws_r20`; the derived record preserves the scope of that finding                            | Passing test suites in the original workspace verifies the code repair, but does not certify executable replay against the redacted paths                                           |
| Target suitability, $\text{chk}_{\text{target,demo}}$ | A use-specific review finds that the transformed context supports the selected schema inspection, corrected edit, and bounded report                            | Admitting these specific target tokens for supervised imitation does not validate other model turns or authorize arbitrary downstream tasks                                         |

: **An Admission Decision for a Derived Recovery Record**: The predicates apply to identified evidence and a specified consumer. A missing required assessment leaves the decision pending or unknown rather than inheriting an unconditional pass. {#tbl-vol3-synthesis-trajectory-roles}

Because each predicate evaluates to true, the pipeline admits the transformed example as a verified decision demonstration. Had path substitution stripped the file names essential for the agent to deduce the correct schema, target suitability ($\text{chk}_{\text{target,demo}}$) would have failed. Furthermore, while this redacted trace is valid for token-level imitation learning, it cannot serve a downstream consumer that requires executable replay, because executing the synthetic paths would require spinning up a fresh environment with matching mock fixtures. A single execution lineage can therefore support fine-tuning while being disqualified from offline replay benchmarks. Neither a valid cryptographic digest nor an overall task pass provides blanket approval across different training regimens.

### Corpus manifest publication {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-manifest-publication}

Admitting `trace_r19_01_redacted_v1` into a storage bucket without binding its target mask, split group, and grader versions leaves a downstream trainer free to supervise the refused edit `e2` by mistake or leak the task into evaluation. Publishing the curated trajectory to the corpus release `repair_demonstrations_v1` prevents that drift by recording every link in the artifact's provenance chain inside the corpus manifest. For this member, the manifest binds the record to its originating run (`collection_run_r19_01`), task identifier, fixture snapshot, candidate code patch, and evaluation grader versions. It references both the transformed trace (`trace_r19_01_redacted_v1`) and the target selection policy (`recovery_targets_v1`), while logging the specific data governance approvals, task group assignments, and split partition versions. Any missing metadata or inactive model dependencies are explicitly tagged as unavailable rather than omitted.

At the corpus level, the manifest catalogs the source data pools, sampling weights, token accounting budgets, domain coverage metrics, and the formal evaluation protocol. Maintaining clear distinctions among raw interaction counts, stored trace tokens, and selected supervised target tokens prevents deceptive accounting. During training, serialization formats and loss masks enforce these target boundaries, ensuring that future trajectory steps never leak into earlier conditioning windows.

This curated trajectory yields a single demonstration artifact. It cannot be repurposed as a preference pair, because the rejected proposal `e2` and the later edit `e4` follow different prefixes (`e4` comes after the refusal and the schema lookup), so they are not alternative continuations of one context. A preference artifact would need competing completions sampled from one saved branch point. Similarly, publishing an environment for reinforcement learning rollouts requires exporting the task fixture, harness configurations, and dynamic graders, rather than static token sequences.

Publishing an immutable corpus manifest establishes a versioned training baseline, which remains separate from deployment governance for any resulting model. Tracking lineage guarantees that if an upstream fixture defect or data privacy request emerges later, pipeline operators can cleanly trace and purge all derived artifacts across downstream model versions. At the infrastructure layer, ephemeral execution sandboxes are destroyed and billed compute charges are settled independently of whether a trace reaches the corpus manifest.

### Cost per emitted artifact {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-cost-per-artifact}

Because every initiated run incurs compute and verification charges whether or not it reaches the manifest, raw trial volume is a deceptive metric for collection economics. A pipeline may execute thousands of autonomous interactions yet emit only a small handful of usable training samples, as trajectories fail safety filters, duplicate existing task solutions, crash during tool dispatch, or remain stalled in asynchronous evaluation queues. Consequently, systems engineers must evaluate collection economics using the cost per emitted artifact, amortizing all spent compute and infrastructure overhead across the accepted dataset.

For a given collection cohort and accounting cutoff, let $\CollectionCohortCost$ represent the total monetary expenditure incurred across environment provisioning, inference generation, tool sandbox execution, automated verification, human review, redaction transformations, and storage. Let $\EmittedArtifactCount$ denote the number of valid artifacts emitted for a designated consumer by that cutoff. The cost per emitted artifact is defined as

$$\CostPerEmittedArtifact=\frac{\CollectionCohortCost}{\EmittedArtifactCount},\qquad \EmittedArtifactCount>0.$$ {#eq-cost-usable}

The numerator $\CollectionCohortCost$ captures all unproductive runs, rejected proposals, and pipeline failures; if a cohort yields zero usable artifacts ($\EmittedArtifactCount = 0$), the pipeline registers the incurred financial loss without dividing by zero. Structurally, @eq-cost-usable mirrors the cost per accepted task formulation (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task): the unit cost equals the average cost per attempt divided by the end-to-end emission yield. This metric isolates data acquisition efficiency, distinguishing curation costs from both runtime inference serving and subsequent model fine-tuning.

```{python}
#| label: lego-14-the-economic-cost-of-contaminated
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COST PER EMITTED LEARNING ARTIFACT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-flywheel-synthesis, @tbl-vol3-curation-cohort-dispositions,
# │          @nbk-14-the-economic-cost-of-contaminated.
# │ Goal: Price the output manifest without dropping other cohort dispositions.
# │ Show: Accounted attempts, emitted-artifact yield, and cost per artifact.
```
